title: Modelling and control
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn how to understand and shape the behaviour of dynamic systems you will meet throughout mechanical, mechatronics, and aerospace engineering. The unit follows a clear model, analyse, and design progression: you begin by describing physical systems mathematically, then explore how those systems actually behave, and finally learn how to influence that behaviour through feedback control. Along the way, you will become comfortable moving between transfer function, state-space, and block diagram representations, and interpreting system responses in both the time and frequency domains. Computational tools are used throughout to help you test your intuition, visualise behaviour, and strengthen your engineering reasoning as you make informed design decisions. This unit gives you the foundation you need for advanced studies in control and dynamic systems, and for your later capstone projects.
learning_outcomes: Record and structure technical notes to support understanding, communication, and independent learning in engineering contexts.
Construct mathematical models of engineering systems, analyse their stability and dynamic behaviour, and apply feedback control principles to meet specified performance requirements.
Use computational tools to simulate, interpret, and reason about the behaviour and control of engineering systems.
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester, typically comprising a mixture of 3-6 hours of scheduled learning activities and 6-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning, and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment, and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Numerical methods and machine learning
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: This unit conveys the fundamentals of numerical analysis techniques and their application to data analysis and the solution of engineering problems. You will be introduced to programming structures, use of AI in programing, software documentation, version control and data management, profiling and hardware optimisation, conventions of scientific computing, numerical errors and stability, techniques for interpolation, integration, the solution of ordinary and partial differential equations, and principles of machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Assess the suitability and limitations of machine learning for current and emerging engineering applications, demonstrating awareness of future directions in engineering practice.
Demonstrate effective use of numerical analysis and machine learning tools to develop defensible solutions to open-ended engineering problems.
Apply appropriate mathematical and numerical techniques to solve common engineering problems, and evaluate program performance, error, stability, and accuracy.
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of 3-6 hours of scheduled learning activities and 6-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Computational fluid dynamics
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is a well-established analysis, design and optimisation approach for industrial fluid and heat transfer problems. Examples include turbomachinery, vehicle aerodynamics and aeronautics. It is also a powerful research tool and is being increasingly used to answer fundamental questions in a wide range of fields, from astrophysics to nanomaterials. This unit provides you with an introduction to this mathematically sophisticated discipline. This involves a review of the equations governing motion and energy of fluids, the mathematical properties of these equations and the relevance of such properties to obtaining numerical solutions. The basics of numerical discretisation and solution methods will be discussed. The unit will also introduce you to using commercial CFD packages in analysing complex industrial problems involving fluids.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the main approaches used to discretise the compressible and incompressible fluid flow equations.
Apply a theoretical understanding of the concepts of resolution, stability and order of numerical methods for solving partial differential equations relevant to engineering.
Appraise the capabilities and limitations of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) packages to model engineering problems in fluid flow and heat transfer.
Execute suitable approximations when modelling turbulent flows.
Formulate an approximate solution to an engineering problem using a CFD package, with appropriate selection of boundary conditions, grid size and turbulence model.
incompatibilities: MEC4447: Computers in fluids and energy
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of 3-6 hours of scheduled learning activities and 6-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Dynamics 1
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces the fundamental principles of kinematics and kinetics as applied to particles and rigid bodies. You will explore concepts of displacement, velocity, and acceleration in rectilinear, curvilinear, and projectile motion, and develop the ability to formulate equations of motion in different coordinate systems. Through analysis of forces and motion in planar mechanisms, you will apply kinematic and kinetic principles to understand the behaviour of translating and rotating bodies. The unit also extends these concepts to the principles of work, energy, impulse and momentum, and provides an introduction to the mechanical vibration of dynamic systems.
learning_outcomes: Determine the motion of particles and rigid bodies in translating and rotating systems by applying the principles of work, energy, impulse, and momentum.
Analyse forces and motion in planar mechanisms by applying kinematic and kinetic principles.
Apply project management principles to plan, monitor, and reflect on time utilised throughout the semester to support effective study practices and continuous improvement.
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester, typically comprising a mixture of 3-6 hours of scheduled learning activities and 6-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning, and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment, and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Composite mechanics
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will be introduced to composite lamina and composite laminates, as well as the mechanical performance of composite structures. You will learn methods for hygrothermal strain and hygrothermal stress analysis of composite structures, and examine failure theories for a composite lamina, micromechanical analysis of a composite lamina, classical lamination theory for composite laminates, and failure analysis of composite laminates. You will then apply these techniques to the intelligent design of tailored composite laminates with specific structural properties.
learning_outcomes: Design composite laminates to meet strength, stiffness and cost requirements for aerospace applications.
Identify, describe and evaluate the properties of fibre reinforcements, polymer matrix materials and commercial composites.
Determine the strength and stiffness of composite laminate structures.
Formulate a model to present the mechanical properties of different combinations and orientations of lamina and laminates.
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of 3-6 hours of scheduled learning activities and 6-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Finite element analysis
faculty: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will be introduced to finite element analysis (FEA) in computer-aided design, including the formulation of finite elements. You will study first-order and second-order elements, the stiffness matrix, integration points, and stress recovery, as well as concepts of convergence and mesh refinement. You will then apply FEA techniques to plane stress and plane strain problems, axisymmetric problems, nonlinear materials, contact problems, large deformations, dynamic problems, and fracture mechanics.
learning_outcomes: Identify the basic theories and concepts of advanced solid mechanics, such as nonlinear materials, contact mechanics, finite deformation and fracture mechanics.
Apply a commonly-used commercial software to carry out finite element analyses on different structural problems.
Identify the basic theories, terminologies and concepts related to the application of the finite element method in computer-aided design of structures, including aircraft structures.
Generate finite element models for truss structures, plane stress, plane strain, axisymmetric and general 3D structural problems.
Select correct element types and designs proper mesh to obtain accurate results from a finite element analysis.
incompatibilities: MAE4426: Finite element analysis and composite structures
workload_hours: The minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of 3-5 hours of scheduled learning activities and 7-9 hours of independent study per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher-directed learning, peer-directed learning and online engagement. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment and preparation for scheduled activities.

title: Spoken English for higher education
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on enhancing your proficiency in verbal communication in academic and professional settings. It aims to develop your confidence, clarity and effectiveness in delivering speeches, presentations, and contributing to academic and professional discussions. This unit covers essential aspects of public speaking and presentation skills in higher education, as well as vocabulary and grammar. You will learn to craft well-structured and compelling presentations tailored to specific contexts, ensuring you communicate with confidence and impact.
learning_outcomes: construct and present compelling arguments for different types of speeches.
demonstrate confidence and clarity in delivering speeches using appropriate tone, gestures, and eye contact
develop and deliver well-structured, engaging, and persuasive speeches tailored to specific audiences and purpose
workload_hours: Minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of scheduled learning activities and independent study. Independent study may include associated readings, assessment and preparation for scheduled activities. You are expected to complete all pre-class activities prior to your scheduled class, and post-class activities should be completed after your scheduled class. Learning activities may include a combination of teacher directed, peer directed and online engagement activities.

title: Management 101
syllabus_overview: This unit is concerned with principles of managing business organisations. Management is important to organisations’ business and survival. The dynamic nature of today’s organisations means that managers require certain knowledge, skills and competencies to manage organisations effectively. The aim of this unit is to provide you with an introduction and overview of management within organisations. The unit will examine management principles, concepts and theories of management, and give you an appreciation and understanding of various challenges facing managers in organisations in today’s competitive global environment.
learning_outcomes: apply the concept of planning, organising, leading, controlling, organisational environment, managerial ethics and corporate social responsibility in organisations
demonstrate the importance of motivation, individual and teamwork associated with the field of management.
identify the nature, scope and functions for management
explain concepts, principles and theories related to the study of management

title: Accounting 101
syllabus_overview: This unit provides you with a foundational understanding of financial accounting principles and procedures. It covers key concepts such as bookkeeping, financial statement preparation, and financial analysis. You will develop essential skills in recording transactions, understanding financial reports, and applying accounting principles in business scenarios. Assessments include individual and group projects, tests, and financial analysis exercises to enhance practical application. By the end of the course, you will be able to compute financial statements, interpret financial data using key ratios, and apply accounting concepts to real-world business situations.
learning_outcomes: identify each business situation using accounting concepts and conventions
apply bookkeeping skills and accounting concepts in preparing the adjusted financial statements.
compute the important elements of financial statements for sole proprietorship
examine financial information by computing profitability, liquidity, and solvency ratios to interpret financial performance

title: Introduction to data analysis
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to the fundamental concepts and methods of data analysis, with an emphasis on organising, summarising, and interpreting data for business and management applications. You will develop skills in descriptive statistics, probability, and basic data handling, and will learn to apply Excel for data organisation, visualisation, and simple analysis. By the end of the unit, you will be able to collect and summarise data, calculate and interpret key statistical measures, and perform introductory probability and survey analysis, providing a strong foundation for more advanced statistical techniques in Year 2.
learning_outcomes: classify and describe types, sources, and levels of data, and organise them using appropriate tables, charts, and Excel tools
design a simple questionnaire and conduct a survey to collect and summarise business data using descriptive statistics
interpret and analyse business data through hypothesis testing and regression analysis to support decision-making.
apply basic probability and conditional probability rules to solve simple business-related problems

title: Marketing 101
syllabus_overview: This unit has been designed to provide you with an introduction to the field of marketing. The unit focuses on the relationship between organisations and consumers, expressed through the marketing mix. Essentially, studies are concentrated on the nature and behaviour of supplying organisations, nature and behaviour of the consumer and the various marketing mix elements (product, price, place, promotion) which are used by organisations to identify and satisfy the needs and wants of consumers. The unit will examine marketing principles, concepts and theories, and give you an appreciation and understanding of various challenges in organisations and consumers in today’s competitive global environment.
learning_outcomes: apply the concept of STP (Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning) and marketing mix in organisational environment.
explain concepts, principles and theories related to the study of marketing
identify the nature, scope and functions for marketing

title: Introductory mathematics for business
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed for students pursuing a career in business. It provides the required mathematical concepts essential for business decision-making and problem-solving. The topics covered include algebraic methods, functions, series, financial mathematics, optimization techniques, probability and applications in business operations. The goal is to equip you with the skills to use mathematics in real-world business scenarios.
learning_outcomes: explain financial concepts and perform related calculations and graphical analyses using mathematical methods
manage priorities while applying entrepreneur and analytical skills to solve business maths problems and make financial decisions.
apply mathematical functions, optimisation, matrices, and inequalities in business operations
identify algebraic and financial mathematics principles used in business decision-making

title: Effective Communication 1
syllabus_overview: This unit provides you with foundational skills in written and spoken communication for academic and business purposes. Emphasis is placed on expressing ideas clearly, using appropriate tone and structure, as well as understanding audience and context. You will engage in individual and group tasks to develop effective communication strategies, build intercultural awareness, and reflect on your own communication practices. The unit also introduces essential processes such as drafting, revising, and responding to feedback to support ongoing improvement.
learning_outcomes: reflect on and revise communication practices to enhance clarity, structure, and impact.
collaborate effectively with others through shared communication tasks and respectful interaction
produce clear and purposeful written and spoken texts suitable for different audiences and contexts
apply key principles of communication to a range of academic, professional, and social situations

title: Economics 101
syllabus_overview: Economics 101 is an introduction to fundamental concepts, principles, and methods in economics. You will be provided with the skills and knowledge necessary to pursue further studies in the field of economics at a tertiary education level.
learning_outcomes: identify basic economics concepts and indicators used in the studies of economics
analyse economics issues of various economics environments.
explain economics concepts, data, graphs and variables used in economics studies
apply appropriate economics concepts and calculations in various economics situations

title: Effective communication 2
syllabus_overview: Effective Communication 2 introduces you to the fundamentals of communication and writing, focusing on clear expression, critical thinking, and effective presentation skills. You will explore verbal, non-verbal, and visual communication, analyse media messages, and develop structured arguments. Through practical activities, you will enhance your writing, research, and public speaking abilities. By the end of the unit, you will be able to apply communication strategies effectively in both academic and real-world contexts.
learning_outcomes: recognise and describe key ideas in communication and writing for academic and everyday use
explain how verbal, non-verbal, and visual communication shape meaning and perception
use effective writing, research, and presentation skills to share ideas clearly and persuasively
evaluate and apply communication strategies to engage effectively in different situations.

title: Volunteering in practice
faculty: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
school: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
syllabus_overview: The unit is focused on developing confidence and capacity to make a positive impact on society through participating in, and leading, volunteering activities. It will focus on exploring conceptual frameworks and ideas that relate to volunteering work, while also exploring ways to apply these in practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on the role of volunteering in contributing to the development and expression of personal and professional identity.
Demonstrate understanding of the volunteer/not-for-profit sector and its connections and contributions to the local, national, and international community.
Demonstrate understanding of the varied nature of volunteering and its contributions to the social, political, and economic life of the Australian community.
Demonstrate understanding of ethical and regulatory issues relevant to volunteering and the volunteer/not-for-profit sector.
Identify and apply appropriate conceptual tools in volunteering/not-for-profit sector settings.
workload_hours: Minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of asynchronous learning activities and independent study. (Minimum 24 hours placement).

title: Global Immersion Guarantee program
school: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
syllabus_overview: The Global Immersion Guarantee is a funded, field-work centred unit exploring the links between the environment, society and technology. Drawing on and experiencing in-country case studies as examples, you will travel to one of nine locations including China, Fiji, India, Indonesia, Italy, Malaysia, Samoa, Vanuatu or Vietnam. During your time overseas you will learn about the human impact on the environment, and the many ways in which this can manifest itself. You will undertake fieldwork with partner organisations that focus on areas such as climate change, food and water security, conservation and urbanisation, overtourism, fast fashion, eco-tourism, the impact of key regional economic sectors on the local environment, global supply chains and environmental sustainability. The fieldwork components of this unit will allow you to apply the theoretical knowledge you learn in class to real world problems. You will be required to complete work prior to, during and after your time overseas. This work will combine online and face-to-face learning and engagement. Before you go, you will undertake a series of online lessons on Moodle that will help you develop your problem framing and reframing skills, your intercultural competence, the theoretical concepts you will apply while overseas, and a good introductory understanding of the country you will be visiting. While overseas, you will engage with, and learn from, local organisations leading solutions to sustainability challenges. You will complete a series of lectures and seminars, and draw on field work to complete an in-country group assessment. After your immersion experience, you will need to complete two major assessment tasks that will prompt you to reflect on your overall experience, and to apply the theoretical frameworks examined in each location.
learning_outcomes: frame and reframe a problem with clarity.
communicate effectively in both written and oral formats;
recognise and explain the key ideas, themes and concepts of development and sustainability in relation to your GIG location.
assess the role, intent, and interaction of local and regional stakeholders in relation to the sustainability challenge explored in your GIG location;
reflect and apply your own intercultural competency skills.
work collaboratively to apply interdisciplinary knowledge in the interpretation and solution of real-world issues;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Identifying and Reframing a Challenge – Team Presentation

workload_hours: Minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 288 hours per semester typically comprising a mixture of scheduled learning activities and independent study. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher directed learning, peer directed learning and online engagement.

title: Research, experimentation and discovery
faculty: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
school: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
syllabus_overview: Research, Experimentation and Discovery (RED) is an immersive educational experience that invites students to bring diverse disciplinary expertise and perspectives to bear on the challenge of how research is implemented into practice. In RED, you will explore and investigate the cutting edge ‘live’ research happening throughout Monash: from responding to the impacts of climate change, preserving geopolitical security and fostering thriving communities. In RED, we invite you to step into these real-world research narratives where you will be tasked to investigate how an interdisciplinary research project can make a difference in and for the world. Across an intensive experience based in a range of on and off campus collaboration spaces, you will be asked to respond to a project in collaboration with a Monash research partner and develop a strategy to translate this research into practice, creating change and impact in the world. In doing so, RED aspires to help you as an emerging professional - no matter your degree or background - to create impact, and lead global, generational change.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect upon your own individual disciplinary perspectives in an interdisciplinary research setting, and in the context of your individual emerging professional identity.
Communicate and disseminate outcomes of interdisciplinary research projects in both traditional and non-traditional formats.
Develop a strategy that responds to an interdisciplinary research challenge that could create real-world impact within broader society.
Analyse a complex interdisciplinary research challenge, considering multiple stakeholders and disciplinary perspectives.
Work collaboratively in interdisciplinary teams to respond to a complex research challenge.
Articulate key principles of interdisciplinary research, while drawing upon perspectives that are both within and outside your own discipline.
workload_hours: 144 hours, made up of intensive workshops, group work and personal learning.

title: Monash Innovation Guarantee
faculty: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
school: Office of the DVC Student Experience and Senior VP
syllabus_overview: The Monash Innovation Guarantee is an intensive unit designed to equip you with the holistic skills and mindsets required to lead innovation solutions. You will work on a purpose-driven solution to a real-world challenge facing a commercial or social enterprise, a government or UN agency, or a start-up. Based in a range of on and off campus collaboration spaces, you will be guided through a three-week innovation process involving analysis, design, testing, validation, and pitching. The Monash Innovation Guarantee provides a solutions-focused experience to transform your capacity to drive change. It provides a basis for understanding how to intervene in contemporary global issues facing industry, and the implications for society.
learning_outcomes: communicate effectively to industry partners from different sectors
collaborate to integrate and leverage interdisciplinary knowledge to approach real-world issues
analyse an industry challenge, considering relevant stakeholders and systems
reflect upon your role in the project, in the context of your emerging professional identity.
apply innovation methods and mindsets to design purpose-driven solutions
workload_hours: 144 hours, made up of intensive workshops and personal learning.

title: Quality and safety in wound care
faculty: School of Clinical Sciences at Monash Health
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: You will explore essential aspects of skin and wound care management, focusing on quality and safety to ensure optimal person-centred outcomes. You will learn the core principles of wound care and how to apply them in various aged care settings. You will also recognise and classify different wound types, understand frameworks for assessing quality and safety, and apply evidence-based wound management principles. In this unit you will learn how to emphasise person-centred care to improve healthcare outcomes and provide strategies to prevent wounds, particularly in at-risk populations, with practical preventive measures to enhance care.
learning_outcomes: Outline relevant frameworks for assessing quality and safety in skin and wound care and discuss their role in improving care for those in aged care settings.
Recognise and classify wound types in older populations.
Explain how person-centred wound care improves healthcare in the aged care sector.
Explain the concepts of quality and safety in the context of skin and wound care management.
Describe the fundamental principles of skin and wound care and how they can be applied to individuals in a range of aged care settings.
Describe basic evidence-based principles of wound management and explain their application in aged care settings.
workload_hours: 8 hours of teacher directed study per week, 8 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 16 hours

syllabus_overview: The MIG is an intensive unit designed to equip you with the holistic skills and mindsets required to lead and implement viable innovation solutions in industry. You will work on a purpose-driven solution to a real-world challenge facing a commercial or social enterprise, a government or UN agency, or a start-up. Industry and academic experts will coach and guide you and your interdisciplinary team through a three-week innovation process involving analysis, ideation, design, testing, validation, and pitching. During the program, you will build your employability skills and broaden your professional networks. The MIG provides a solutions-focused experience to transform your capacity to drive positive change in the workplace through multi-stakeholder collaboration and innovation. It provides a basis for understanding how to intervene in contemporary global issues facing industry, and the implications for society and your career.
learning_outcomes: Apply innovation methods and mindsets to design and implement viable and purpose-driven solutions;
Lead and collaborate to integrate and leverage interdisciplinary and multi-stakeholder knowledge to approach real-world issues;
Reflect upon your role in the project, in the context of your emerging professional identity, and create a career and leadership plan.
Analyse an industry challenge, considering relevant stakeholders and systems;
Communicate effectively to industry partners and stakeholders from different sectors;
workload_hours: 144 hours, made up of intensive workshops and personal learning

title: Foundations of health promotion and program planning
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to key principles of, and planning for, health promotion. You will examine health promotion frameworks and theories that are used to promote health at a population level to compliment and contrast individual treatment. You will examine the values and principles that guide contemporary health promotion and its capacity to influence the determinants of health. You will also develop skills in needs assessment, priority setting, using evidence and theory to make intervention choices and program evaluation. The roles played by partnerships, capacity building and participation will be explored, and the steps toward improving program sustainability are examined.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply the key principles, theories and frameworks, used in health promotion and prevention.
Define and explain the history of preventive health and health promotion
Describe and apply the key steps of program planning including needs analysis, participation and the development of goals, objectives and strategies
Identify and adapt a range of approaches for promoting health that include upstream, mid-stream and downstream actions.
Critically reflect on the role of Health Promotion in addressing contemporary and emerging challenges in health.
incompatibilities: PHI5002: Foundations of health promotion and program planning
HSC5020: Foundations of health promotion and program planning

assessment_tasks.task_name: Health promotion and resource rationale (1,200 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week. There is an expectation that students will attend 3 on-campus Block Days incorporating 23 contact hours.

title: Caring for older people: Nutrition and mental health essentials
faculty: School of Clinical Sciences at Monash Health
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: You will gain essential skills and knowledge to support the nutritional and mental health needs of older adults in community and aged care settings. You will explore the physical, psychological, and social aspects of normal ageing. This includes understanding the specific nutritional challenges faced by individuals in aged care and the impact that this has on families, informal carers, and formal care providers. You will also learn about common mental health disorders in older populations, with an emphasis on their biopsychosocial factors. You will recognise cultural and community-specific perspectives of mental health and learn about approaches and services that align with the diverse needs of older adults. By integrating knowledge of nutrition, mental health, and culturally sensitive care, you will learn to promote the well-being of older adults and support those involved in their care.
learning_outcomes: Outline common mental health disorders in older adults, highlighting their biopsychosocial factors and implications in community and aged care settings.
Describe the factors that influence food choices and nutritional needs in older adults, including the impact of ageing on nutritional capacity and health outcomes.

Discuss and communicate strategies to promote successful ageing and positive well-being, integrating proper nutrition, mental health support, and practices that enhance physical, cognitive, and social health in older adults.
Identify the role of healthcare workers and caregivers in supporting the physical and mental health needs of older adults, including the provision of adequate nutrition and mental health care.
Discuss the dietary requirements of older adults, including those with health conditions and comorbidities, and the impact that this has on families, informal carers, and formal care providers.
Discuss the relationship between nutrition and mental health in older populations and explore services and strategies to support both aspects holistically.
Identify the physical, psychological, and social aspects of normal ageing and discuss factors associated with successful ageing.

Recognise the importance of cultural diversity in shaping approaches to mental health and nutrition in older populations, ensuring culturally sensitive care practices and community-specific perspectives.
workload_hours: 8 hours of teacher directed study per week, 8 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 16 hours

title: Introduction to epidemiology and biostatistics
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Differences between descriptive & analytical epidemiology, strengths & weaknesses of different epidemiological study design & basic concepts & methods of biostatistics including confidence intervals, p-values & sample size, statistical tests for comparing groups, regression models & survival analysis. Design & evaluation of clinical trials.
learning_outcomes: Explain and contextualise the concepts of population, sampling, measurement, bias, confounding and causation;
Explain how disease is measured in populations, calculate,interpret and communicate measures of association and difference;
Use epidemiological and biostatistical principles to critically evaluate and interpret and communicate findings from epidemiological research.
Demonstrate an understanding of basic concepts and methods of biostatistics.
Interpret confidence intervals, p-values and sample size and communicate their meaning.
Critically analyse the strengths and weaknesses of different epidemiological study designs;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Development activities (5 x critical reflections 420 words each. Total 2,100 words)

title: Evaluating public health programs
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Program evaluation is important for measuring the effect of public health programs and determining their influence on longer-term health outcomes. It also provides valuable evidence to improve the delivery, reach and impact of public health strategies. This unit will enable you to design evaluations that are suitable for a range of public health and disease prevention programs. You will conduct evaluation planning based on theoretical approaches and best-practice principles. Levels of evaluation will be examined, as well as the range of quantitative and qualitative data collection methods suitable for the different contexts and stakeholders involved in public health practice. The unit will equip you with the skills to choose appropriate methods for data collection, as well as use suitable evaluation frameworks, tools and resources specific to public health and disease prevention programs. There will be exploration and discussion of the evaluation challenges posed by the complexities of public health action and the contexts in which it is carried out.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and investigate how evaluations measure the effect of public health programs, and explain the importance of evaluations in terms of influencing long-term public health outcomes.
Apply design features to various public health programs, including critically evaluating differing theoretical approaches to evaluation design.
Create an evaluation plan that is tailored to a specific public health program, which critically communicates the scope of the evaluation and how it will be delivered.
Distinguish the different levels of evaluation, and consider how they work together to provide a comprehensive assessment of a program.
Select evaluation methods appropriate to an evaluation design, including applying tools and resources specific to public health promotion.
Construct evaluation designs to measure public health programs that are specific to stakeholder priorities and objectives.
workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week. There is an expectation that you will attend 3 on-campus Block Days.

title: Introductory biostatistics
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to biostatistics as applied to public health and management studies. Biostatistics is the science of describing, summarising, and analysing health-related data. It is essential to understand biostatistics in order to design, conduct, and interpret health-related research. The basic principles and methods used in biostatistics are covered in this unit. This includes the technical qualifications necessary for analysing and interpreting data on a descriptive and bivariate level. Topics include classifying health data; summarising data using simple statistical methods and graphical presentation; sampling distributions; quantifying uncertainty in results from a sample; working with statistical distributions; comparing two or more groups/methods using confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (p - values); assessing the association between an outcome and an exposure using the chi-squared test; using risk comparisons (RR and OR); predicting an event or identifying risk factors for an event of interest where the event is measured on a continuous scale or a binary scale (yes/no).
learning_outcomes: Analyse data using a specific software package.
Present data using relevant tables, graphical displays, and summary statistics, quantify uncertainty in study results.
Classify data into appropriate measurement types.
Formulate research hypotheses into a statistical context in public health studies.
Accurately interpret statistical methods and results reported in health publications.
Estimate quantities of interest and evaluate hypothesis with appropriate statistical methods.
workload_hours: ONLINE mode: 2 hours online seminar (recorded), 2 hours online live tutorial, 2 hours online guided discussion, and 6 hours independent study per week. ON-CAMPUS mode: 4 face-to-face contact hours (2 hours seminar and 2 hours tutorial), + 2 hours online guided discussion, + 6 hours independent study per week.

title: Introductory epidemiology
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is taken concurrently with MPH5041, as together they are prerequisites for clinical epidemiology elective units. Upon completion of this unit you will be able to measure frequencies of disease i.e. incidence, prevalence, "population at risk"; and measure associations in epidemiological studies; different study designs i.e. observational studies, experimental study designs; bias associated with study designs, misclassification, confounding and effect modification. You will critically appraise different epidemiological studies, apply diagnostic and screening tests, and examine outbreak investigation.
learning_outcomes: Explain and contextualise the purposes of descriptive and analytical epidemiology;
Interpret and communicate the results of epidemiological studies; and
Evaluate the adequacy of exposure assessment in epidemiological studies;
Solve complex problems relating to the use of epidemiological concepts and study designs.
Critically analyse epidemiological papers from the medical research and OHS literature;
Analyse the strengths and weaknesses of different epidemiological study designs;
Explain and contextualise the concepts of study questions, population, sampling, exposure assessment, bias and confounding;
workload_hours: 12 hours per week including two-hour weekly workshops for 10 weeks.

title: Planetary health
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will examine the health impacts of climate change, and the relevance of this to the principles and practices of public health. Informed by an understanding of the fundamental role of climate stability for sustained population health, and of evidence for anthropogenic global warming, the focus of the unit will be on direct and indirect mechanisms through which climate change affects health, including extreme weather events, changing patterns of vector-borne disease, water-borne infections, food quality and availability, air quality, and social disruption. There will be an emphasis on evidence for past and predicted health effects, health burden magnitude and distribution, and the complex interplay between population and environmental factors that influence vulnerability. You will apply this knowledge to critically appraise adaptation and mitigation initiatives from a public health perspective and will be expected to engage with current climate change issues and communicate your ideas clearly and effectively.
learning_outcomes: Identify the social and environmental factors that influence the vulnerability of populations to the health impacts of climate change.
Describe the causes and impacts of climate change
Critique public health responses to the impact of climate change on health.
Analyse the implications of climate change for public health (including the impact on mental health, infectious disease, food and water security, natural disasters and severe weather events).
Design adaptation and mitigation responses to the impacts of climate change.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group oral presentation (5 mins per student - speaking)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week, plus 3 on-campus Block Days.

title: Demographic methods
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit gives you a solid foundation in formal demography, where quantitative data and techniques are used to calculate demographic measures. Topics include sources of demographic data and assessment of their quality; calculation and interpretation of basic measures of fertility, mortality and migration; population dynamics, growth and ageing; life tables; Indigenous demography; and population projections. Learning activities include hands-on calculation and interpretation of demographic measures using real-world data. You are expected to be familiar with Microsoft Excel.
learning_outcomes: Choose appropriate demographic methods to calculate demographic measures.
Interpret demographic measures in the context of changing populations.
Calculate and graphically present demographic measures. .
Identify, locate and critically evaluate quality of different types of population data.
Effectively communicate demographic measures and their interpretation in written, tabular and graphical form to a lay or policy audience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Lexis diagrams and life tables (900 words or equivalent)
Migration and family formation (1,500 words or equivalent)
Indigenous demography and models of population structure (1,500 words or equivalent)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher directed learning activities and 6 hours of self-directed study per week. 12 hours of self-directed study per week.

title: Research methods
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an introduction to the research methods used in observational studies and is designed to help you develop the practical skills required in the design and assessment of a research project. It covers issues in protocol design, including study type selection, introduction to questionnaire design, sampling methods, and ethics approval. This will introduce you to planning data management and statistical analysis and developing a study budget. An introduction to the role of qualitative research is also covered.
learning_outcomes: Describe and demonstrate how information may be collected from people and transformed into usable data for scientific study;
Design and present a research protocol to answer the stated question using observational study designs;
Identify, evaluate and communicate when qualitative methodologies may be useful; and
Pose a research question answerable by observational study methods used to examine public health;
Demonstrate the ability to participate and communicate effectively within a group.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Critical reflections (6 x case scenarios, 600 words)

title: Regression methods for epidemiology
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Confounding and effect modification, logistic regression, conditional logistic regression for matched case-control studies, linear regression, diagnostics to assess model fit, model estimation methods, Poisson regression for rates, Stata statistical software.
learning_outcomes: Analyse epidemiological data using statistical software on a laptop computer.
Apply regression methods to epidemiological data.
Discuss critically the regression methods used in published articles on epidemiological research studies.
Interpret regression methods in terms of the epidemiological concepts of confounding and effect modification.
Estimate sample size requirements in the context of simple regression modelling.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Poisson regression data analysis and evaluation (1,000 words)
Linear regression data analysis and evaluation (1,800 words)
Logistic regression data analysis and evaluation (1,800 words)

workload_hours: Sem 1 - DE mode: 24 contact hours over 3 block days + 2 hours online tutorial + 2 hours online guided discussion + 6 hours independent study per week.

title: Environmental influences on health
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Environmental influences on health including physical, chemical and biological hazards as well as principles of assessment, management and control of environmental health risks.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate techniques for exposure assessment and risk assessment;
Identify important chemical, physical and biological hazards in the environment and analyse related risks to health from environmental factors in Australia;
Evaluate evidence-based interventions to manage common environmental risks and reduce harm.
Communicate fluently using appropriate terminology about hazards, risks and risk management interventions in a variety of contexts, including community engagement, and;
Critically appraise the epidemiological literature which informs the evidence base for environmental health risk control strategies;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written assignments (1 x 2,000 words; 1 x 2,500 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours off campus, self-directed learning per week, 4 hours teacher directed learning per week, plus 20 contact hours over 3 block days.

title: Chronic disease: Epidemiology and prevention
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Chronic non-communicable diseases represent a major global public health challenge. They affect lives of people, their families and communities. This unit provides learners with an overview of surveillance of chronic diseases, social determinants of and risk factors for chronic non-communicable diseases. Learners will discuss epidemiology and strategies for prevention of major chronic disease groups impacting Australia including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, respiratory disease, musculoskeletal disorders, mental illness and injury. Learners will gain practical skills for describing the epidemiology and burden of chronic diseases, assessing risk factors and analysing strategies for chronic disease prevention.
learning_outcomes: Examine the influence of social and economic factors on chronic diseases
Analyse strategies for the public health control of chronic diseases.
Describe the epidemiology and burden of chronic diseases in Australia
Assess risk factors and causal pathways leading to important chronic diseases.
Evaluate the role of public health evidence in the control of chronic diseases.
Evaluate methods to measure the health impact of chronic diseases
incompatibilities: PHI5207: Chronic disease: Epidemiology and prevention
workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week, plus 2 on-campus Block Days.

title: Introductory health economics
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an introduction to health economics. For many of you, this will be the first time you may have studied economics so we have developed the course with this in mind. We will cover topics including - Why is the discipline of economics relevant to healthcare? Key economic concepts such as opportunity costs, marginal analysis efficiency, and the concept of benefit. Basic microeconomic tools for health economics including, demand, supply, markets, market failure, and the role of governments. The Australian healthcare system from an economic perspective including structure and expenditure. The role of health insurance and different funding mechanisms in health care. Important public healthcare policy topics from an economics perspective including the reform of Medicare and efficiency in sub-sectors of the healthcare system (such as primary care and hospitals).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate health care challenges and policies from an economic lens.
Explain the unique characteristics of healthcare which make the application of standard market based economic theory problematic. including the role of governments.
Evaluate different health financing methods in terms of created incentives and disincentives.
Compare health care markets and markets in other sectors.
Define key economic concepts, including efficiency, opportunity cost, utility, costs and benefits.
Explain the role that governments can play when standard economic theory fails.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Final Assessment (8-10 min Oral Presentaion and 3,100 words written essay)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including a combination of synchronous and asynchronous lectures, videos, zoom sessions, and tutorials. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Qualitative research methods
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an introduction to the research designs and methods used in qualitative research and is designed to help you develop the practical skills required in the design and assessment of a qualitative research project. The unit covers the six main qualitative research designs relevant to public health and health services research, data collection methods, analysis approaches and critical appraisal of qualitative studies. Ethical considerations and mixed methods approaches are also covered.
learning_outcomes: Describe principles of good research and ethical issues in qualitative research including recruitment, sampling, data collection and analysis approaches;
Critique qualitative papers published in health services and public health literature;
Develop qualitative data collection processes (interview and focus group guides, participant observation sheets);
Describe the main types of data analysis approaches for qualitative research (content analysis, thematic analysis, narrative analysis, discourse analysis and grounded theory);
Apply thematic analysis coding techniques to an example transcript;
Match the research question to the appropriate qualitative research design (descriptive, phenomenology, action research, case study, ethnography and grounded theory);
Describe how qualitative research can be used in mixed methods research designs.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Ethics application (1,000 words) including study protocol (2,400 words)
Interview or focus group guide (1,800 words)

workload_hours: 3 on campus block days. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 8 hours

title: Infectious diseases: Epidemiology and prevention
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Importance of transmission source, host and organism factors in infectious disease epidemiology. Outbreak investigation, surveillance of infectious diseases, prevention/control strategies, mathematical modelling of infectious diseases and of impact of immunity. Includes discussion of infection control, vaccines, exotic and emerging diseases.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of mathematical modelling in relation to infectious diseases.
Argue the importance and dynamic nature of infectious diseases;
Identify the unique aspects of infectious disease epidemiology and evaluate these aspects in practice;
Critically evaluate the epidemiologic principles underlying disease control and prevention strategies;
Critically evaluate the epidemiologic principles underlying disease surveillance programs;
Critically evaluate strategies in the prediction, detection and control of infectious disease outbreaks;
incompatibilities: PHI5218: Infectious diseases: Epidemiology and prevention

assessment_tasks.task_name: Four critical reflections (4 x 400 words each. Total 1,600 words)
Leder disease assignment (short answer 1,000 words and Infographic -1 page)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed and 6 hours of self-directed study per week. There is an expectation that you will attend 3 on-campus Block Days incorporating 22 contact hours.

title: Determining value for money in health care
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: You will be introduced to the basic concepts, methods and applications of economic evaluation in the healthcare sector. Topics include the different methods of economic evaluation (e.g. cost-minimisation analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis, cost-utility analysis, cost-benefit analysis); the strengths and limitations of studies and study design; analysing the quality of evidence; how economic evaluation differs from other forms of evaluation; and how information from an economic evaluation can aid decision making. Practical applications include when to undertake an economic evaluation, designing an economic evaluation, the steps in conducting an economic evaluation; and the tools and methods for measuring costs and outcomes and analysis.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the different methods of undertaking an economic evaluation
Explain the essential characteristics of economic evaluation, and how it differs from other forms of health care evaluations
Explain the basic steps in conducting an economic evaluation of a health care intervention
Calculate the main results from economic evaluations using incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, cost-effectiveness planes, the net benefit approach and acceptability curves
Analyse the different methods of presenting health outcomes in an economic evaluation
Explain the different types of cost that will be included in an economic evaluation and how to measure and value these costs
incompatibilities: HEC5973: Economic evaluation in health care

assessment_tasks.task_name: Multiple choice quizzes (4 x multiple choice quizzes each with 10 questions)
Data analysis, reporting and interpretation (2,100 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher directed study per week, including combination of synchronous and asynchronous lectures, videos, zoom sessions and tutorials. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Health and safety risk management leadership and governance
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will undertake a comprehensive exploration of core Health and Safety risk management concepts, risk assessment techniques, and decision-making processes. You will gain a deep understanding of the principles, framework, and process of ISO 31000 risk management standards, including assurance activities. The unit emphasises the comparison and contrast of ISO 31000 risk assessment processes with existing governance and compliance approaches. Additionally, you will learn to communicate the critical importance of engaging stakeholders in risk assessment and the implementation of effective controls. Upon successful completion of this unit, you will be proficient in demonstrating, explaining, comparing, and communicating key aspects of risk management, preparing them for advanced roles in Health and Safety risk management.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the importance of engaging stakeholders in Health and Safety risk assessment activities including implementing effective controls.
Plan, critically evaluate and apply various Health and Safety ISO 31000 risk assessment processes in alignment with existing governance and compliance approaches.
Describe core Health and Safety risk management concepts, risk assessment techniques and decision-making processes.
Critically evaluate and apply the principles, framework, and process of ISO 31000 risk management standards including assurance activities.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Integrated case-based learning and assessment (ICLA) (up to 1,800 words)

workload_hours: 10 hours of off-campus study per week, including: 6 hours self-directed-online learning & 4 hours teacher-directed online learning per week; and 3-day block of face-to-face learning, on-campus.

title: Clinical trials
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The term "clinically proven", used throughout even the lay vernacular, highlights the high status of clinical trials in health research. This is because clinical trials provide the most robust evidence of the benefits of healthcare interventions; they are the 'gold standard' study design. A solid understanding of clinical trials is a key requirement for anyone working in clinical research, or who need to interpret the results of clinical research. This unit will equip you with the skills to formulate research questions, design appropriate clinical trials, select and recruit study subjects, conduct randomisation, analyse data, interpret findings, manage outcomes and consider issues of ethics, budget and quality assurance. It will also endow you with the skills to critically appraise clinical trials.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise a published clinical trial in order to determine its validity or otherwise to real-life practice and policy.
Investigate the practical considerations of undertaking clinical trials, including planning, gaining ethics approval, recruitment and retention of subjects, measurement of outcomes and data analyses.
Explain the importance of communication between key stakeholders in clinical trials.
Critically analyse the theoretical approaches to clinical trials, including different types of clinical trials, and the strengths and limitations of each.
Examine the principles of clinical trials and understand their role in informing healthcare practice and policy.
Formulate a meaningful question that has relevance to clinical practice or public health, design the right trial for the question, and articulate this design in a study protocol.
workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week, plus two on-campus Block Days.

title: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Critical appraisal of literature reviews; problem formulation and protocol development; intra-rater agreement for assessment of relevance; validity assessments; data collection forms; variation between study findings, combining the findings of independent studies, inferences based upon overviews; statistics of meta analysis, Cochrane Collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a systematic review in a small group that conforms to accepted standards;
Develop a protocol (or planned methods) for a systematic review;
Formulate a structured question for a systematic review of randomised controlled trials, and understand the motivations for doing a systematic review;
Assess the quality of systematic reviews conducted by others, and apply the results to clinical practice.
Clearly report the systematic review;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group written report 1 - A protocol or plan of a systematic review of randomised controlled trials
Written report - Critically appraise a published systematic review
Group written report 2 - Systematic review of randomised controlled trials

workload_hours: 12 hours per week comprised of a mix of directed and self-directed learning plus attendance at 3 day block

title: Social and cultural determinants of health
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit explores health, and health outcomes, influenced by culture and society, at individual and population levels. It provides skills to enhance understanding of the perspectives of First Nations Australians ways of knowing, being and doing. The unit also explores culturally and socially diverse communities, focusing on improving health and wellbeing, to enhance experiences and improve impacts of the health and social care systems. It draws on concepts derived from studies of society and culture to identify and discuss relationships between health and wellbeing, and the socio-economic and cultural realities in which people live. The consequences of socio-economic disadvantage, inequality and inequity, and discrimination, and how these can be addressed in health settings, are a key focus.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine and evaluate familiar aspects of culture and society, including historical representation, in order to extend knowledge of the socio-economic and cultural structures, institutions and processes relevant to health at local and global levels.
Develop and apply the social imagination to examine the social and cultural production, construction and organisation of health and wellbeing, locally and globally.

Form an appreciation of how multiple levels of disadvantage based on cultural, socio-economic or ethnic background, gender, or sexual orientation can intersect, leading to further discrimination and subsequent worsened health outcomes.
Apply key principles of social and cultural thought to the lived experience of culturally diverse Australians.
Explore factors affecting health of culturally and socially diverse individuals and populations in Australia.
Apply key principles of social and cultural thought to the lived experience, ways of knowing being and doing of First nations Australians.
Explore factors affecting health of First Nations Australians.
Apply social, cultural and political ideas as analytical tools to critically examine cultural, social, political and economic factors influencing health and wellbeing.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Individual presentation (Maximum of 5 mins with no more than 4 slides)
Guided reflection (1,100 words within 3 days of exercise)

workload_hours: This 6 credit point unit will be delivered over a 12 week semester. There will be six hours of own time tasks per week plus 6 hours of self-directed learning per week. This will include one block days plus online tasks.

title: Introduction to occupational health and safety
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The effects and human cost of occupational disease and injury, occupational health and safety law, worker's compensation, negligence, occupational rehabilitation, historical achievements and challenges, international and national organisations.
learning_outcomes: Contextualise the legal framework applying to the workplace;
Describe the theoretical underpinnings of various injury models and their use within Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems;
Critically appraise contemporary Work Health and Safety (WHS) data sources;
Analyse the human and economic cost and causes of workplace injury and death in Australia
Analyse the WHS impacts of contemporary and changing work patterns and new and emerging challenges.
Communicate the fundamental principles of WHS practice

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study analysis and reflection - end of week 6 (1,200 words)

title: Humans, work and physical hazards
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces physical hazards including noise, vibration, heat, cold, radiation and pressure effects and conditions such as work-related musculoskeletal disorders that are common in workplaces, the effects on human health, and prevention and control measures to improve work health and safety. You will examine and apply a range of approaches to identify and control physical hazards and risks and develop evidence-based recommendations for improving practice.
learning_outcomes: Communicate fluently using appropriate terminology to describe work-related physical hazards and risks and their prevention and control
Apply legislation relevant to physical hazards in the work environment
Apply a range of approaches to identify, assess and control physical hazards and risks including a systems approach, risk management process, the hierarchy of controls, and design of work
Identify common work-related musculoskeletal disorders and preventive strategies
Interpret the assessment results and develop and effectively communicate appropriate recommendations for risk controls.
Identify and analyse the properties and health effects of common work-related physical hazards
prerequisites: MPH5241: Introduction to occupational health and safety
workload_hours: 12 hours per week comprising 6 hours self-directed study/learning per week, plus 4 hours teacher directed learning per week, plus 3 on-campus block days.

title: Workplace hazards: measurement and management
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn about hazards encountered in workplaces, including chemical and biological hazards. You will develop and apply skills to evaluate and measure hazards and the risks they present to workers. You will also learn how to assess and manage such risks in workplaces, enabling workers to do their jobs without undue risk to their health and wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Communicate fluently with diverse audiences about workplace hazards, risks and risk management, using appropriate terminology.
Critically evaluate and apply evidence about the health effects of workplace exposures to inform evidence-based interventions
Assess workplace hazards and understand the principles of measuring exposures, assessing the risks they present and risk management options
Plan, critically evaluate and recommend practical strategies to mitigate risks presented by workplace hazards

assessment_tasks.task_name: Integrated Case-based Learning and Assessment (ICLA) (up to 1800 words)

workload_hours: 10 hours of off-campus study per week, including: 6 hours self-directed-online learning & 4 hours teacher-directed online learning per week; and 3-day block of face-to-face learning, on-campus.

title: Psychosocial work environment
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Psychosocial effects of work on individuals are explained from a preventive viewpoint. You will examine topics including mental health and its effect on employment, alcohol and drug use, disability discrimination, equal employment opportunity legislation, workplace health promotion and shift work.
learning_outcomes: Apply the risk management process to assess and control work-related stress;
Reflect critically on theoretical models of job design and organisational psychology;
Identify common psychosocial hazards and risks in the work environment and impacts on health;
Apply legislation relevant to the psychosocial work environment;
Develop insightful and persuasive evidence-based recommendations to prevent, eliminate or reduce work-related stress and improve workplace culture and practice.
Communicate fluently using appropriate terminology to describe psychosocial hazards and risks and their prevention and control;

7 x Critical reflections (300 words each or 1.5 mins each: Total 2,100)

title: Global health care delivery: principles and  challenges
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will explore global health through a real-world lens. In today’s fast-changing, interconnected world, understanding global health is more important—and more complex—than ever. In this unit you will be invited to explore how health and illness are shaped not just by biology, but by global politics, inequality, and history. You will take a hands-on, human rights–based approach to studying global health care delivery. Together, we’ll look at how globalisation, colonisation, and international governance shape people’s health around the world—and how we might do things better. Key topics include: Why some communities face greater health challenges than others Barriers to health care for migrants and refugees How colonial legacies and international aid affect health systems The politics of neglected diseases and global health funding Real-life case studies of global health successes and failures You will develop skills in critical thinking and intercultural understanding, and gain tools to help tackle the health challenges of our time—wherever you are in the world.
learning_outcomes: Develop intercultural competence in health care
Apply postcolonial frameworks to global healthcare issues
Investigate and critique current governance structures for complex global health issues
Explain human rights based approaches to global health care delivery
Analyse and predict factors contributing to global health inequity
Critically analyse impacts of globalisation on human health and consider the ethics of globalisation
incompatibilities: PHI5252: Global health care delivery: Principles and challenges

assessment_tasks.task_name: Critical reflections discussion forum (6 x 150 words = 900)

workload_hours: 12 hours per week comprised of a mix of directed and self-directed learning plus attendance at 3 day block

title: Injury epidemiology and prevention
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will cover the principles of injury epidemiology, prevention and control. The unit will provide an introduction to the injury epidemiology and prevention field with a particular focus on issues facing injury surveillance, countermeasure development, injury policy and injury burden estimates.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and contextualise the concept of injury as a preventable health condition;
Analyse and evaluate issues in the measurement of injury severity, definition, burden and outcome.
Identify requirements for and conduct injury surveillance;
Analyse and evaluate the strengths and limitations of a variety of research methods used to define the nature and extent of injury;
Develop, implement and evaluate injury prevention programs and frameworks for countermeasure development;
Theorise and analyse approaches to injury policy and legislation; and
Synthesise the principles of injury prevention and control and related models;
Identify and describe the context and consequence of burden of injury;
workload_hours: 5 day intensive block.

title: Health and human rights
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit examines the interrelationship between public health and human rights. It begins by providing an overview of the development, content and application of human rights. Human rights aspects of contemporary local and international health concerns are then considered.
learning_outcomes: Critically apply different human rights approaches to health and understand their strengths and weaknesses.
Discuss the development international human rights instruments, their status, mechanisms for their enforcement and their corresponding practical limitations.
Apply human rights knowledge to a diversity of public health issues including family violence, asylum seekers and indigenous health.
Investigate the different mechanisms by which human rights can shape public health programming and practice generally and their respective limitations.
Explain the interrelationship between human rights and health through exploration of current human rights dilemmas.
Identify the human rights issues of particular situations including complex humanitarian emergencies, armed conflict and particular group issues.
Familiarity with the theoretical foundations of human rights.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Team presentation (5 minutes per student, plus question time)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed readings per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week. 4 on-campus Block Days.

title: Law for health systems
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Review of legal management principles related to health care by examining common law principles and statutes. Examination of the Australian legal system, including the Coroner's court, with an emphasis on Victorian and Commonwealth cases and statutes. Focus on key areas of medical and health law such as negligence consent, privacy of health information, clinical research, abortion, euthanasia, mental health, infectious diseases, health complaints, and law for health facilities such as hospitals.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and transmit knowledge and complex health law principles to health care managers and non-specialist audiences.
Interpret and synthesise the applicability of legal reviews and reports to health care management practice.
Analyse critically, reflect on and synthesise the sources of law relevant to the management health care organisations.
Research and apply legal principles to handling complex clinical situations.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Critical Reflection (6 x 400 words to 5 x 480 words: (2,400 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed learning activities per week, and 6 hours of self-directed study per week, plus 2 block days via zoom.

title: Clinical leadership and management
faculty: Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This Unit will review key leadership, management, and organisation theory and its application to healthcare settings. It will investigate the role of the manager, leadership skills, staffing issues, clinician engagement, performance management, career management, managing change, structuring organisations for patient care, developing strategy, consumer engagement, change management, and project management.
learning_outcomes: Explain the application of complex management theories in the management of health care teams and organisations.
Interpret the applicability of health care research findings to health care management practice.
