learning_outcomes: Develop evidence-based educational materials for the health-related setting.
Apply nutrition knowledge in a health-related setting.
Demonstrate teamwork skills in professional practice.
Reflect on professional practice within a health-related setting.
Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviours in a multidisciplinary health-related setting.
workload_hours: 8 hours of workshop, 8 hours of seminar Internship for 10 weeks, with 40 hours of commitment every week.

title: Nutrition education and counselling
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Emphasis on nutrition education and counselling skills is important in the educational progress of future nutritionists. It requires a combination of nutritional expertise and psychological understanding for nutritionists to work in clinical or community settings. Well-developed nutrition education and counselling programs have been shown to reverse issues related to dietary adherence. In this unit, the students will explore the psychological theories and health models that underpin the understanding of human health behaviours, development of nutrition education and counselling skills.
learning_outcomes: Identify appropriate communication methods in approaching an individual or group for nutrition education or counselling purpose.
Illustrate counselling skills for a target individual or group.
Describe theories and models that influence nutrition education and counselling processes.
Identify components of counselling skills and its influence on individuals.
Exhibit consideration towards the influence of cultural background, experiences, attitudes, and biases that could influence outcomes of nutrition education and/or counselling.
workload_hours: An average of 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 2 hours of lectures, 2 hours of workshops per week and 3 hours of practical every fortnight. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Advanced nutritional physiology and immunology
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The unit takes a systems approach to understanding the human body and integrates knowledge from human biology, anatomy, physiology and basic cell biology to achieve an understanding of bodily functions. It will give you an understanding of the detailed workings of vital body systems, acting separately and together to ensure the integrated function of the body as a whole. There will be a particular focus on the immune system in this unit and the area of pharmacology will be introduced owing to interactions with nutrition and physiological processes. This unit complements the unit NUT2104 (Nutritional Biochemistry)
learning_outcomes: Describe the pharmacokinetics of common drugs, their distribution and metabolism in the body and their interaction with nutrients.
Interpret physiological data generated in the laboratory and demonstrate skills in the reporting of laboratory experiments.
Explain the physiological and biochemical processes associated with the digestion and metabolism of food.
Evaluate current evidence to describe the integration of physiological systems and processes within significant nutrition issues relating to health and disease.
Discuss the role of innate and acquired immunity in health and disease.
Investigate and explain the structure and function of the gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, respiratory, circadian, immune, urinary, skeletal and muscular systems to nutrition, health and disease.
Describe the organisation of the human nervous system and differentiate between the roles of the peripheral and central nervous system in normal physiological functioning.
Explain neuroendocrine control within the body.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentations (Group assessments; Infographic (10%); Recorded Pitch, 5 min (10%))
Immunology, body systems and nutrition enquiry (Part A: Max 1,500 words Part B: 10 mins)

workload_hours: 2 x 2 hours online lectures 2 x 2 hours workshops on campus 1 x 3 hours practical on campus 13 hours self-directed study and assessment Total hours: 24 hours per week

title: Communication in clinical nutrition
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Skills in clinical nutrition communication is important in the educational progress of future nutritionists. It requires a combination of nutritional expertise and psychological understanding for nutritionists to work in the community settings. Well-developed nutrition communication and intervention programs have been shown to reverse issues related to dietary adherence. In this unit, you will explore the psychological theories and health models that underpin human health behaviours and the development of clinical nutrition communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Implement cultural, empathy and professionalism competence when communicating to targeted individual or groups.
Describe theories and models that influence the nutritional communication processes.
Illustrate effective communication skills to individual and group.
Design effective nutrition education and communication resources for targeted individuals or groups.
Apply critical thinking skills when providing clinical nutrition solutions to targeted individuals or groups.
workload_hours: An average of 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 2 hours of lectures, 2 hours of workshops per week and 3 hours of practical every fortnight. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Food: Science, composition and skills
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides a strong foundation in supporting you to become experts in the area of food - from the cellular scientific makeup and composition to food microbiology, food regulations and standards coupled with skill based acquisition, exploring the diversity of food and eating practices with an application to nutrition and dietetic practice. Theme 4 (Food from Science to Systems) is the key theme explored in this unit with integration from Theme 1 (Personal Development and Professional Practice) as you extend your skills in cultural competency and communication and the scientific underpinnings from Theme 3 (Nutrition Fundamentals of Health and Disease). In this unit, you will acquire food preparation skills; become familiar with Australia's diverse foods and modify recipes and menus to meet specific nutritional goals. You will gain an appreciation of micro-organisms and the important role they play in food production and in food-borne disease; becoming proficient in risk assessment and safe food handling practices. They will discuss the regulatory system set up in Australia to control food safety, food labelling and food content and gain experience in evaluating the role of science and politics within the regulatory decision-making process.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in meal preparation, recipe analysis and recipe modification and interpret the influence of portion and serve size to meet specific nutritional goals
Identify macronutrient and micronutrient composition from the main food groups and cultures found in Australia
Describe the diversity of microorganisms and discuss their relationships in the context of food, nutrition, health and disease
Critically evaluate regulations relating to food labelling, food composition and food-related claims in Australia and assess compliance across the food supply
Outline the fundamental principles of toxicology and risk assessment, including HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points), and apply the principles to the setting of food standards.
Demonstrate laboratory techniques required to culture and identify microorganisms within the context of food safety
Describe the format and content of the Australian Food Standards Code and explain the role of FSANZ, Commonwealth and State governments in formulating, implementing and enforcing modern food law

assessment_tasks.task_name: Recipe analysis and modification report (individual - 1,000 words)

workload_hours: Approx 9 hours contact per week 12 x 2 hour workshop (24 hours) 5 hours lecture per week (60 hours) 6 x 2 hour kitchen laboratories (12 hours) 3 x 3 hour microbiology laboratories Approx 20 hours per week including contact hours and private study

title: Nutritional biochemistry
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit aims to provide an in depth understanding of the metabolism of macro and micronutrients and of the role of nutrition in influencing cell growth, cancer development, blood formation and gene function. Emphasis will be on clinical relevance, the integration of biochemical pathways and how this is modulated by dietary change, and on techniques used to assess both normal dietary requirements and nutrient deficiencies. You will be introduced to biochemical mechanisms of energy expenditure and storage, including metabolic adaptation to periods of fasting or food intake.
learning_outcomes: Apply the main biochemical, clinical and physical measures for assessing and interpreting the signs and symptoms of nutrient inadequacy and/or deficiency.
Critique the role of micronutrients in the maintenance of blood health, bone health, as an antioxidant and in excitable nerve cells.
Describe the combined role of macronutrients and micronutrients in maintaining health and the prevention of disease.
Describe the nutritional influences on cell growth, differentiation, programmed cell death and the development of the cancerous cell.
Explain carbohydrate, protein and lipid metabolism in the context of the fed and fasting state, hyperglycaemia and alcohol consumption.
Demonstrate problem based learning skills and the ability to communicate and apply scientific knowledge in relation to nutrition-related scenarios.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group case study presentation (20 mins) and wiki resource (2,000 words)

workload_hours: 2 x 1 hour lectures 2 x 1 hour tutorial every week, 1 x 3 hour practical on 2 occasions

title: Nutrition, activity and health in chronic diseases
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an integrated study of the role of diet in the causation and treatment of chronic diseases that are endemic in westernised societies. It builds upon the scientific concept of disease aetiology explored in Integrated Science Systems (BND2103) and the critical interpretation of scientific literature and research skills developed in years 1 and 2. Learners will explore the epidemiology of the major nutrition related diseases, their causal pathways and population based recommendations for prevention. The rationale for the application of dietary modifications for patients with specific disease states and the means of evaluating dietary treatment is explored. Nutrition related emerging issues in disease aetiology and management are also explored and the emphasis on the important role of genetic susceptibility in nutrition science is continued. Student centered teaching and learning methods will be used to support the delivery of the unit content. Students' participation as adult learners will be encouraged through the curricula with emphasis on extending their scientific communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Assess the role, benefits and limitations of diet, activity and lifestyle in aetiology, prevention and management of chronic diseases.
Communicate nutrition messages and evidence relating to chronic disease prevention and management using contemporary approaches.
Evaluate the efficacy of population-based interventions to manage chronic diseases.
Apply epidemiology, medical and nutritional principles in the nutritional assessment and management of chronic lifestyle related diseases conditions.
Appraise the functional role of nutraceuticals in disease management and prevention.
Discuss emerging trends in diet related disease risk and treatment approaches.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Critical review (Written report: 2000-2500 words OR Recorded presentation with notes)

workload_hours: Lectures: 3-4 hours/week, Tutorials: 1 hour/week, SDL: 10 hours/week.

title: Nutrition controversies
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Nutrition controversies will focus on developing your fundamental scientific knowledge and critical reasoning skills in the area of nutritional science. You will build on your skills gained in earlier units that taught principles relating to evaluation of evidence and advanced research methodologies. Using your background in physiology, immunology and biochemistry, you will link diet and disease outcomes using available evidence. In this unit you will develop an appreciation for the controversial and unresolved nature of the reported associations between dietary factors and disease processes. You will critically evaluate the underpinning evidence and identify unresolved questions and/or alternative opinions. Examples of nutritional controversies will be drawn from topics studied across the range of other units on the course and from current topics and trends in the media and on social media. Teaching activities in this unit will have an emphasis on student-centred enquiry supported by a series of student-led seminars and discussions, and written and oral research syntheses.
learning_outcomes: Formulate an objective analysis of the scientific evidence supporting or refuting conflicting viewpoints on diet-disease relationships.
Collaborate effectively in a multi-disciplinary team to achieve optimal outcomes in nutritional science.
Synthesise evidence from the literature, reflecting on various perspectives, to determine scientific significance and impact in nutrition.
Appraise novel scientific studies in relation to controversial nutrition topics and related media.
Communicate assertively in written and oral formats using scientific and non-technical language where appropriate.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral presentation (5-min oral presentation plus 1,000 words)

workload_hours: 3 hours of teacher directed study per week as a 3 hour workshop and 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 9 hours

title: Nutrition assessment
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: Monitoring and evaluation are essential components of determining nutritional status at both the individual, community and population level. The interpretation of anthropometry, biochemistry, clinical, dietary and environmental information (ABCDE framework) is therefore central to the work of nutrition scientists. In this unit, you will examine the methodological applications and limitations of nutrition assessment approaches used with individuals, communities and populations in varying contexts. You will be enabled to critically employ research and analytical skills when interpreting and evaluating nutrition assessment data, including identifying appropriate methods in terms of precision, validity, feasibility and reproducibility. The unit will also develop your ability to apply relevant guidelines, policies and recommendations to estimate nutritional requirements for populations and to support evidence-informed decision-making. You will be exposed to a range of methods across the ABCDE framework, as well as nutrition screening tools routinely used in clinical, research and population health settings.
learning_outcomes: Apply the nutrition assessment framework from individuals to populations.
Apply appropriate guidelines, policies and recommendations to estimate nutritional requirements for populations.
Evaluate methodologies used in nutrition assessment.
Apply appropriate guidelines, policies and recommendations to estimate nutritional requirements for populations.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Interpreting anthropometry and body composition summary (2,000 word equivalent)
Nutrition Assessment Portfolio: 2 x 45-minute online quizzes

workload_hours: On-campus: 6 hours per week of interactive lectures and workshops + 6 hours self-directed learning and completion of assessment tasks.

title: Applied sport and exercise nutrition
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is focused on you developing knowledge, skills, and competencies to critically evaluate current developments in sport and exercise nutrition, targeting both health and sports performance outcomes in a variety of populations. The scientific disciplines of exercise physiology, biochemistry and immunology will be emphasised as you critically evaluate the underlying evidence supporting benchmark nutritional guidelines and recommendations given to individuals/groups partaking in exercise. Laboratory sessions will provide practical experience of various anthropometrical, nutritional and hydration assessment techniques; alongside applying knowledge of area specific theories into practice through a kitchen laboratory session. Particular reference to the roles and responsibilities of the sport and exercise nutrition expert when working in multi-disciplinary teams will be emphasised.
learning_outcomes: Assess nutritional, hydration and exercise requirements for active individuals performing at different sporting activities and levels and develop appropriate exercise and nutrition regimes;
Evaluate nutritional and hydration assessment techniques in sport and exercise;
Critically appraise the evidence base to justify food, fluid, supplement and other management strategies for improving sport and exercise performance.
Appraise the effect exercise and the environment have on various body systems and body composition;
Evaluate the role of macro- and micro-nutrients in human energy transfer systems active during different types of exercise, and recognise the nutritional implications;
workload_hours: 12 x 2 hour per week lectures/tutorials on campus, 12 x 2 hour per week seminars on campus (delivered twice, seminar groups A and B), 3 x 3 hour practical sessions (physiology, hydration, kitchen lab) - (delivered twice, seminar groups A and B). 36 hours self-study and formative/summative assessment related work.

title: Work placement
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will complete a professional work placement within the field of nutrition science, applying your academic knowledge and skills in a real-world setting. You will have the opportunity to work alongside experienced professionals, contributing to nutrition projects and work tasks. Throughout the placement, you will apply relevant nutrition science knowledge, skills and evidence within an organisational context. You will create innovative solutions to real-world nutrition problems, collaborate effectively with key stakeholders, and demonstrate professional behaviours. You will also gain insights into your future career as a nutrition professional through the practice of critical reflexivity.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional behaviours to an appropriate discipline standard.
Collaborate effectively with key stakeholders in workplace environments.
Apply relevant nutrition science knowledge, skills and evidence within an organisation.
Create innovative solutions to real-world nutrition problems.
Apply critical reflexivity to personal and professional development as a nutrition professional.
prerequisites: NUT2102: Food: Science, composition and skills
NUT2002: Applied research methods in nutrition

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral presentation and reflective diary (10 minutes + 1000 words)
Written Assignment – Project Analysis (2,000 words max)

workload_hours: 16 days on applied work placement. 8 hours of in-person workshops (4 x 2hr sessions) and one full day of project presentations end of semester (week 12).

title: Food systems and planetary health
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit explores the interconnected relationships between human health, environmental sustainability, food systems and the living ecosystems that we depend on. You will learn about food system activities from paddock to plate, including agricultural production, food distribution, processing, retail, consumption and waste. You will explore drivers that influence these food system activities, including globalisation, climate change, industrialisation, colonisation and commercialisation and examine how these currently undermine efforts to achieve a healthy, sustainable and equitable food system. You will be exposed to a variety of perspectives on planetary health, including First Nations perspectives, food industry stakeholders and public health experts. You will examine the way you personally interact with the food system and conduct an audit of the built, social, economic and natural food systems in a Local Government Area. You also will identify and explore innovative opportunities for nutrition professionals to improve the food system and contribute to the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.
learning_outcomes: Examine interconnections between food, nutrition, climate change and planetary health in the context of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.
Analyse activities within the food supply chain, comparing and contrasting industrial and local food system practices.
Examine the impact of colonisation and demonstrate respect for Indigenous peoples’ knowledges regarding food systems and planetary health.
Examine the current food system through a social justice lens to achieve equitable access to nutritious food.
Critically evaluate the political, economic, social and environmental drivers of global and local food systems
Evaluate opportunities to innovate and disrupt current food systems practices to promote planetary health.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Planetary Health Communique (500 word critique and 800 word re-written article) - Individual
Food system audit (2,000 word report: 20% and 15 minute oral presentation: 15%) - Group
Sustainable table challenge (2,000 word structured reflective piece) - Individual

workload_hours: On-campus: 4 hours per week of interactive lectures and workshops + 8 hours self-directed learning and completion of assessment tasks.

title: Precision and personalised nutrition
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this unit is to enable you to explore the molecular mechanisms by which nutrients and other food components affect metabolism and cell function. The unit focuses on the biochemical role of essential nutrients in metabolism, their role in the aetiology of major chronic diseases with postulated nutritional involvement in disease mechanisms. This unit will reinforce the concepts of nutritional genomics and epigenetics by presenting relevant examples from recent scientific literature and provide you with the competence to interrogate on-line gene databases to answer real life questions. Additionally, the unit will explore the concept of the gut microbiome and its interaction with the diet.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the interaction between food components, the gut microbiome, and genetic factors that influence biochemical pathways and health and susceptibility to disease (Nutrigenetics and Epigenetics).
Explain the role of nutrients and other food components in the modulation of gene expression on a global scale (Nutrigenomics and Epigenetics)
Explain the fundamental concepts of genetics and the application of genetics to molecular biology research
Integrate and generate biochemical and nutritional science knowledge in professional context such as personalised nutrition
Explain the biochemical roles of the essential nutrients in metabolism

assessment_tasks.task_name: Wiki page and group presentation (2,000 words)

workload_hours: 2 hours face-to-face/online/week 2 hours computer workshops/week 2 hours teacher - directed learning/week

title: Contemporary development in nutrition
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will explore a broad range of current topics in nutrition, addressing both local and global contexts. You will also seek recent scientific evidence to debunk nutrition claims commonly found on social media. Throughout the unit, you will evaluate contemporary nutrition issues and synthesise evidence to support or challenge current nutrition practices. You will develop the ability to appraise scientific literature from reputable sources, integrate evidence, and communicate your findings effectively for both academic and public audiences.
learning_outcomes: Integrate independent and teamwork-based problem-solving skills to address nutrition-related issues.
Communicate nutrition concepts effectively, both orally and in writing, for academic and public audiences.
Evaluate contemporary nutrition issues within local and global contexts, and propose evidence-based solutions.
Synthesise and integrate evidence to debate current nutrition practices, policies, or claims.
Appraise scientific literature from reputable sources to address complex and emerging nutrition-related controversies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Debunking false nutrition claims on social media (10 min)
Debate (10 min individual presentation and 5 minutes to respond to peers' points)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 3 hours of lectures and 3 hours of workshops. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Internship 2
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The unit forms a key element of Theme 4 – Research and Practice in Nutrition. It gives you the chance to apply what you have learned throughout Years 1, 2, and 3 in nutrition, food, and medical sciences within a real-world workplace setting. You will be responsible for identifying and securing a suitable placement site, as outlined, before the commencement of the internship. You will work independently and within a team to design and deliver an evidence-based nutrition program tailored to the needs of your host organisation. This is your opportunity to gain valuable, hands-on experience and insights into the daily work of a professional nutritionist. You will be supported and monitored by the university supervisor and on-site supervisor(s) who will guide your progress. To successfully complete the unit, you must ensure that an approved placement site has been secured prior to the start of the internship. You must fulfil at least 640 hours of placement and meet all academic requirements. These include assessments conducted by your on-site supervisor and the university supervisor. Through this unit, you will enhance your practical skills, build professional confidence, and prepare yourself for a career in the field of nutrition.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professionalism and ethics in a multidisciplinary team within a workplace.
Demonstrate active participation, teamwork and contribution in a workplace environment.
Apply advanced nutrition knowledge in a workplace setting.
Communicate nutrition information through evidence-based nutrition practice in a workplace setting.
Foster reflective practice to promote continuing professional development in a complex workplace setting.
Develop, implement, monitor and evaluate a nutrition intervention program at the workplace.
workload_hours: 8 hours of workshop and 8 hours of seminar Internship will be held for 16 weeks, with 40 hours of commitment every week.

title: Food and nutrition policy
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will explore how food and nutrition policies influence public health, with a focus on Malaysia’s national nutrition strategies. You will analyse policies addressing key issues such as malnutrition, obesity, and food security, while also evaluating global approaches to nutrition governance. Throughout the unit, you will engage in case studies, policy analysis, and discussions, enabling you to develop evidence-based policy recommendations that consider economic, cultural, and environmental factors. By applying critical thinking and research skills, you will learn to propose innovative solutions to nutrition-related challenges. By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the analytical, policy evaluation, and communication skills needed to contribute to nutrition policy development and advocacy. This course will prepare you for a future in public health, policy analysis, and food system management in Malaysia and beyond.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the local and global food policy in addressing the nutritional related challenges
Propose evidence-based policy recommendations to improve nutritional outcomes, considering economic, cultural, and environmental factors.
Analyse the role of local food and nutrition policy in shaping public health outcomes
Communicate key findings of the case study based on the relevant policy.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study presentation (report 1,800 words, presentation 15 mins)

workload_hours: 18 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 6 hours of lectures, 3 hours of tutorials, 6 hours of Workshops and 3 hours of Seminar. 18 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 18 hours (Teacher directed) + 18 hrs (Student directed) =36 hours/ week Teacher directed: 18 hrs x 4 weeks = 72 hrs Student directed: 18 hrs x 4 weeks = 72 hrs

title: Applied research in nutrition
faculty: Jeffrey Cheah School of Medicine and Health Sciences Malaysia
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit forms the core element of Theme 4 – Research and Practice in Nutrition , building on knowledge and skills drawn from Theme 1, 2 and 3. In this unit, you will learn the necessary skills and knowledge to conduct an applied research project in the area of human nutrition. Your learning within this unit will cover a comprehensive range of topics, including research methodologies, data collection and analysis, and the application of research findings to practical nutritional problems. Throughout the unit, you will engage in hands-on projects stimulating real-world research scenarios. By the end of the unit, you will have developed a thorough understanding of the research process in nutrition and be well-prepared to contribute to the field through your own research endeavours.
learning_outcomes: Justify theoretical knowledge and skills in designing a contemporary research project.
Evaluate research findings based on currently available scientific evidence.
Practice effective professional performance by applying research skills to communication, problem-solving and teamwork.
Rationalise the choice of research methods implemented in a particular research project.
Examine ethical requirements when conducting research.
Synthesis new knowledge gained from research project and apply to professional practice.
Analyse and interpret research data in accordance with accepted research standards for various settings.
Communicate research project in various formats to a variety of audiences.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral presentation (15 min presentation and 5 min Q&A)

workload_hours: 3 hours of lecture / week, 3 hours of workshop / week, 8 hours of seminar Applied sessions for 10 weeks, with 16 hours of commitment every week. 18 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 36 hours

title: Public health nutrition
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will review the concepts and approaches of population health in the context of nutrition. The content will explore current public health nutrition practice issues related to priority issues such as obesity, food security and the food supply. A systems based, health promotion framework to addressing priority nutrition issues will be discussed and current public health nutrition practice will be evaluated. Students will explore the political foundations of public health policy in Australia including the impact of public health policies and will develop skills in policy analysis and public health advocacy. This unit will provide students with the foundations knowledge in preparation for the development of skills of the practice of public health nutrition. The key theme explored in this unit is Theme 2: Determinants and influences on population health and nutrition coupled with partial integration of content from Theme 4: Food: from science to systems.
learning_outcomes: Apply a socio-ecological, systems based approach to understanding and managing population nutrition issues.
Evaluate how public health policy may influence food consumption and nutrition status.
Explore opportunities for beneficial social, environmental and nutritional change to the Australian food supply.
Employ best practice frameworks and approaches for planning, implementation and evaluation of these issues in the development of nutrition interventions.
Describe the current key public health nutrition priorities and issues in Australia and the policy frameworks that support these.
Explain the use of and process of public health advocacy and apply the advocacy framework to a current public health nutrition issue.
Appraise the political, environmental, social and economic influences on public health nutrition goals and practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Public health nutrition program plan (2,500 words)

workload_hours: Week 1 - 12: 3 hour interactive workshops and 3 hour pre/post class activities, and self-directed study.

title: Foundations of dietetic practice
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to the profession of dietetics, commencing your pathway to becoming an expert in food and nutrition and a safe, effective and reflexive healthcare professional. This unit is tailored for the non cognate path for Masters of Dietetics (96CP) under the course architecture project. Students coming through the cognate path (the Monash Uni BNut. Sc.) will receive credit for this subject and be eligible to proceed into the 72 CP Masters program. This unit includes interactive learning and teaching (including hands-on learning experiences - e.g. field trip) within a smaller class size to support your transition into the program. A variety of topics are explored in this unit including: the Australian food supply system, food knowledge and application, nutrition assessment, nutritional requirements across the lifespan; research skills; professionalism, self-awareness and cultural responsiveness; and additional elements to support your development towards becoming a dietitian. Concepts of health education and promotion will enhance your' knowledge and ability to communicate nutrition messages effectively to groups and individuals as well as support your collaboration and teamwork. You will be introduced to reflective practice and complete a professional portfolio to support your personal and professional development.
learning_outcomes: Formulate dietary and lifestyle recommendations for individuals and groups, integrating an applying and evidence based approach.
Integrate psychological, cultural, personal, economic, environmental and social factors in formulating dietary and lifestyle recommendations for individual and groups.
Apply nutrition and dietary assessment tools and methodologies to inform clinical reasoning and care planning in nutrition and dietetic practice.
Apply critical thinking and foundational research skills and knowledge to support evidence-based nutrition and dietetic practice.
Integrate the theoretical basis of health communication, health education and health promotion to planning, implementing, facilitating and evaluating behaviour change.
Discuss knowledge of food, food products, food preparation methods, food systems and sustainability and translate in developing dietary recommendations for clients and communities.
Critically reflect on own culture, values, beliefs, attitudes, biases, assumptions, privilege and power at the individual and systems level
prerequisites: NUT3002: Nutrition, activity and health in chronic diseases

assessment_tasks.task_name: Nutrition group education (2000 words + 20min video recording)

workload_hours: On Campus: This unit will run over one semester with an average of 24 hours per week allocated to both contact and private study with the majority of time dedicated to contact hours. For example: 8 hours of lectures and tutorials 4-8 hours of private reading/self-study 4-8 hours preparation for and contribution to tutorials.

title: Introduction to nutrition and dietetics practice
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to the practice of nutrition and dietetics. You will develop a comprehensive understanding of the role of the dietitian in utilising nutrition in the prevention and management of disease across the continuum of care and a range of communication strategies. The unit will also provide significant opportunities for you to investigate and develop personal and professional identities and will extend your ability to reflect on skills required for professional practice. An introductory placement in a health care setting will allow you to develop understanding of the roles of the dietitian within the healthcare system, practise core dietetic skills and work as a member of an interdisciplinary team.
learning_outcomes: Integrate critical reflection and reflexivity, effective professional and personal communication skills and teamwork to illustrate problem solving.

Employ core dietetic practice skills, including data collection and interpretation, assessment, communication and intervention strategies to formulate, implement and evaluate effective person-centred nutrition care for the treatment and prevention of disease.
Apply understandings of dietetic roles and practice across the continuum of care, from individuals to populations.
Practice safely and professionally, as part of a dietetic and inter-professional team.
Synthesise and communicate evidence-based findings and translate these into dietetic professional practice.
Examine personal and professional identity and professionalism for dietetic practice and integrate these into personal and professional learning.

Apply nutrition counselling theory and utilise a range of communication strategies in developing practical, relevant and targeted nutrition conversations and interventions for diverse audiences across the continuum of care.
prerequisites: NUT5004: Food systems for nutrition and dietetic practice
NUT3002: Nutrition, activity and health in chronic diseases
workload_hours: 2hrs per week recorded lectures and reading own time over 10 weeks (pre-class) = 20hrs 8hrs per week workshops (4 x 2hr workshops) real time over 10 weeks (in-class) = 80hrs 2 x 3hr and 1 x 1hr clinical simulation practical activities = 7hrs* *Please note that this is the actual contact time you will have for clinical simulation practical activities. These activities will be timetabled for 3 x 8hrs but you will be allocated to a set timeslot in groups.

title: Professional practice: Community and public health nutrition and food systems
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is a placement experience that will challenge you to integrate your academic training and synthesise knowledge to plan, implement and evaluate a practical community/public health nutrition program that considers the associated food system. Placements are undertaken as a group in an organisational setting (e.g, health, welfare, local government, not-for-profit, social enterprise, education) to address an identified nutrition related priority issue identified by, and relevant to the placement organisation. As a group, you will be responsible for the project design, collection and analysis of data and synthesis of findings into deliverable outputs for the organisation. This unit will allow you to develop the professional skills required for nutrition and dietetic practice across a range of community and public health settings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the social, environmental, economic and political determinants of nutrition status for a priority public health nutrition area.
Acknowledge and reflect on your own culture, values, biases and privileges, and their influence on professional practice.
Develop and practice effective partnerships, networks and collaborations with a range of inter-professional teams and personnel.
Advocate for policy and practice change to benefit health and nutrition outcomes for a population.
Adopt a curious and critical approach in all aspects of professional practice.
Illustrate effective negotiation and conflict management skills while undertaking professional practice.
Appraise the social, cultural, economic, environmental and sustainability factors that impact on a population group(s) food availability and food access within a food system.
Apply professional leadership to communicate and promote the importance of food and nutrition across diverse settings
Evaluate professional practice and make plans for continuing learning and development.
Plan, implement and evaluate evidenced based population health approaches and solutions to prioritise nutrition issues across community settings.
workload_hours: 30-38 hours per week for 7 weeks plus an additional 5 days project orientation and in semester sessions.

title: Advanced nutrition and dietetics practice
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with the foundational skills needed for effective clinical case management, with respect to a range of clinical conditions and diseases. The emphasis and focus of the learning opportunity will be on providing person centred care through dietetic education and patient case management. You will be provided with opportunities to learn through simulation and case-based learning platforms. Further to this, the key focus of this unit is to ensure that you are able to demonstrate professional competencies as outlined by the Dietitians Association of Australia.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and apply evidence-based approaches to individual patient case management

Integrate knowledge of science and disease into nutrition assessment and management of individual cases including consideration of broader issues regarding healthcare systems and provision, management, ethics and quality improvement.
Evaluate the role of diet in the aetiology, prevention, and management of a range of clinical conditions and diseases.
Integrate theories into counselling and education, including behaviour change, to support effective person-centred individual patient case management.
Integrate personal, social, clinical, cultural, physiological, ethical, environmental and economic factors into clinical reasoning and decision making in individual patient case management.
Formulate effective individual case management plans (including prioritising care and discharge planning), drawing on core skills in the dietetic process.

Apply a range of methods and strategies to communicate effectively, clearly and concisely to diverse audiences, adapting or co-creating communication messages for specific audiences across areas of practice

assessment_tasks.task_name: Clinical handover and case discussion (15 minutes)

workload_hours: This unit will run over 7 weeks with an average of 22 hours per week allocated including own time and in class study as outlined below. 8hrs per week recorded lectures, reading and own time activities (pre-class) = 56hrs total 10hrs per week (5 x 2hrs) workshops on campus (in class) = 70hrs total 3 x 8hr workshops (full days) off campus (public health hospitals) = 24hrs total 1 x 2hr tutorial (interprofessional learning) on campus = 2hrs total

title: Applied research skills in nutrition and dietetic practice
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop capabilities to undertake practice-informed research in the field of nutrition and dietetics. You will identify and investigate a contemporary nutrition and dietetic issue of public health or clinical significance. Through critical engagement with scientific literature, you will collect, analyse, and interpret research evidence to inform evidence-based practice. Your emphasis, in this unit, is placed on translating research findings into practical applications for diverse stakeholders, including health professionals, organisational leaders, communities, advocacy groups and policymakers. Throughout the unit, you will demonstrate ethical and professional behaviours in research conduct, and apply both critical and creative thinking to evaluate complex challenges in nutrition and dietetics practice. By the end of the subject, you will be able to contribute meaningfully to research, practice, and policy in nutrition and dietetics, supporting improvements in individual and population health.
learning_outcomes: Apply research and quality management approaches to address real-world challenges in nutrition and dietetics.
Integrate ethical, personal and professional behaviours consistent with evidence-based research principles and the codes of nutrition and dietetics practice.
Illustrate digital literacy when addressing nutrition and dietetics issues, and utilising technological driven platforms.
Apply advanced teamwork, communication and collaboration strategies to contribute effectively within a research team, to advance nutrition and dietetics practice.
Disseminate research findings to inform evidence-based nutrition and dietetics practice, research, and advocacy.
prerequisites: NUT5008: Pathways to practice: Building your nutrition and dietetics career
NUT5005: Professional practice: Individual case management and food systems
NUT5002: Professional practice: Community and public health nutrition & food systems

assessment_tasks.task_name: Research Dissemination Artefact (1,500 words 4-6 minutes video or audio)
Contemporary Nutrition Issues Research Review (2,500 words & 4 minutes).

workload_hours: The unit will run over 5 weeks. Each week will comprise 8 hours of workshops, 8 hours pre-post class learning (including online modules), and 12 hours self-directed learning.

title: Food systems for nutrition and dietetic practice
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will extend your knowledge of the food systems that exist within organisations, and the role of the dietitian in ensuring that food and eating experiences are safe, nutritious and enjoyable and goals of the organisation are achieved. It will develop your skills in planning eating experiences, cooking, monitoring food environments, measuring quality indicators, advocating for change, communicating information and applying the technical, business and policy elements that support an organisation to function. You will explore a range of organisational food systems including the university campus, stores and retail settings, hospitals, residential aged care, community meals and commercial food businesses. Teaching and learning are designed to be interactive and hands-on, delivered through weekly workshops and practical activities including field trips, fieldwork and kitchen practicals. The theory learnt in this unit will be applied and built on in food systems activities integrated into placement in other units. This unit will prepare you to perform a range of tasks that are critical for employment and entrepreneurship in a range of work contexts.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the system-level principles of organisational management, human resources, financial management, change management, quality improvement, sustainability and policy in activities that support nutrition and dietetics practice.
Evaluate the factors that make and influence organisational, local and global food systems.
Apply entrepreneurial mindset, marketing, management and business skills to nutrition and dietetics practice.
Utilise a variety of communication strategies to engage different audiences across a range of settings.
Critique changes needed within organisational food systems to better support indigenous people
Apply technical, culinary skills and food composition knowledge to support dietetic practice in organisational food systems.
Evaluate elements of organisational food systems using relevant standards, policies and/or tools.
prerequisites: NUT5001: Introduction to nutrition and dietetics practice
NUT3002: Nutrition, activity and health in chronic diseases

assessment_tasks.task_name: Business plan proposal (3,000 words and 5 min video, group 4-5 students)
Menu assessment plan and report (2,000 words, individual)

workload_hours: 4 hours of workshops per week 2 hour of fieldwork practical activities per week 6 hours of self-directed study including pre and post class activities 2 x 3 hour kitchen practicals per semester Total per week = 12-15 hours

title: Professional practice: Individual case management and food systems
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is a placement experience that will support your progression and fulfilment of entry level competencies in individual case management and foodservice management. You will be placed in health care contexts and develop skills in nutrition assessment, planning, management and monitoring of individuals, and exploring and improving food, food service and eating environments at the systems level. This unit will allow you to develop the skills required for nutrition and dietetic practice at the individual and systems level across a range of institutional care settings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate person-centred counselling skills to negotiate and facilitate nutrition, behaviour and lifestyle change and empower clients with self-management skills.
Evaluate professional practice and make plans for continuing learning and development.
Utilise a collaborative care approach by working effectively as a member of the dietetic and broader healthcare team to demonstrate mastery of person-centred dietetic practice.

Apply specialised knowledge of science, nutrition, diet and disease into assessment, diagnosis, intervention, monitoring and evaluation of individual cases in a healthcare environment including the provision of safe, high quality, nutritious and sustainable food.
Apply an evidence-based approach to support individual case management and critically evaluate effectiveness of intervention compared to best practice in dietetics.

Demonstrate person-centred dietetics care across a range of cases which includes the ability to formulate, implement and evaluate effective individual case management including prioritising care, working with the inter-professional healthcare team and discharge planning.

Exhibit oral and written communication skills and conflict resolution skills in professional interactions with nutrition and dietetics peers, colleagues, patients/clients and other stakeholders in the healthcare and academic environment.
Deliver effective counselling and education skills to support dietetic case management to the patients/client/family/carer and healthcare team.
Explore, evaluate and propose solutions to systems-level challenges in food service settings and food systems to support both individual case management and organisational goals of operation.

Integrate personal, social, clinical, cultural, dietary, economic, environmental, ethical, medical and physiological factors into clinical reasoning and decision making in individual dietetics case management in the healthcare environment.
prerequisites: NUT5003: Advanced nutrition and dietetics practice
NUT5004: Food systems for nutrition and dietetic practice
NUT5001: Introduction to nutrition and dietetics practice
workload_hours: You will spend the majority of time for this unit allocated to a healthcare setting (10 weeks of either 4 or 5 days per week placement within a health care setting, plus up to 18 hours of on campus workshops on non-placement days). You will also be expected to attend tutorials and presentations in the academic setting (scheduled around placement commitments) with the remaining time allocated for private study. You are expected to attend placement for the equivalent of full time hours during your scheduled placement weeks. It is also expected that you undertake private study outside of placement hours. Placements may extend into non standard university semester time.

title: Pathways to practice: Building your nutrition and dietetics career
faculty: Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This capstone unit supports your transition from academic study to professional practice in nutrition and dietetics. It offers a structured opportunity to consolidate your learning, reflect on personal and professional development, and explore diverse career pathways. You will strengthen your capabilities in culturally safe and responsive practice, in working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. A key focus is on enhancing employability through the identification and articulation of your individual strengths, values, and competencies, and how these influence and impact on your professional practice. You will develop practical skills in gaining employment, workforce readiness, and professional communication, while also engaging with innovative and entrepreneurial approaches to dietetic practice. The unit also emphasises lifelong learning, encouraging you to identify future learning priorities and develop strategies for your ongoing professional growth. To support targeted professional development, you will choose specialised areas of interest and undertake additional learning to deepen your preparation for practice.
learning_outcomes: Integrate innovative and entrepreneurial approaches to dietetic practice, including problem-solving, leadership, financial literacy, and service development in traditional and emerging areas of dietetic practice.
Evaluate personal and professional capabilities to inform a commitment to lifelong learning aligned with evolving career goals, professional identity, and competency standards.

Evaluate the impact of how colonisation and systematic racism, social, cultural, behavioural and economic factors affect Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ health outcome and how this might influence dietetic practice and outcomes.
Evaluate own culture, values, beliefs, attitudes, biases, assumptions, privilege and power at the individual and systems level, and their influence on professional practice.
Articulate critically own transferable skills that enhance employability across diverse learning and practice contexts.
Analyse contemporary trends and expectations in dietetic practice to inform reflective career planning and produce tailored, professional application materials.
Synthesise and communicate insights from personal and professional learning to articulate evolving values, goals and perspectives of dietetic practice.
prerequisites: NUT5005: Professional practice: Individual case management and food systems
NUT5002: Professional practice: Community and public health nutrition & food systems
NUT5007: Applied research skills in nutrition and dietetic practice
workload_hours: The unit will run over 5 weeks. Each week will comprise 8 hours of workshops, 8 hours lectures/learning modules online, and 12 hours self-directed learning.

title: Professional issues in occupational therapy
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn about the unique role of occupational therapists in comparison to other healthcare professionals. You will develop the skills required to demonstrate appropriate behaviour and beginner-level proficiency in occupational therapy professional skills such as communication, manual handling, activity analysis and occupational health and safety. You will gain an understanding of the professional behaviour, legal, cultural, and ethical considerations that are imperative in occupational therapy practice. The unit will also expose you to various simulated scenarios and case studies to equip you with the necessary skills to understand the challenges faced by clients and consumers of healthcare services.
learning_outcomes: Articulate, examine, and demonstrate the application of occupational health and safety considerations for settings where occupational therapists practice (i.e., infection control, hand hygiene, risk management);
Demonstrate competency in practice education skills relating to manual-handling, equipment use, and correct use of mobility techniques;
Analyse and reflect on concepts of disability and its impact on individuals, families, carers, and significant others;
Demonstrate emerging verbal, non-verbal, and written communication skills for occupational therapy practice;
Articulate, evaluate, and demonstrate understanding of professional behaviours and ethical and legal issues pertinent to a practicing occupational therapist;
Apply task and activity analysis to the occupational therapy practice context.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Objective Structured Professional Skills Exam (OSPSE) (40 minutes)

workload_hours: Lecture component: 2 hours per week, Tutorial/Practicum component: 2 hours per week, Private study: 8 hours per week.

title: Foundations of occupational therapy practice
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn about occupational therapy's historical origins and theoretical foundations. Using case studies and practical learning activities, you will explore and apply theoretical concepts, models, and frameworks to understand and guide the professional reasoning processes in occupational therapy practice. You will gain an understanding of the principles and mechanisms underlying the relationship between people, their environment, and their daily occupations and how this relates to human health and well-being. You will develop foundational knowledge of the psychometric properties of occupational therapy assessments and measures, which will help you understand their quality, relevance, and usefulness in professional practice. While completing this unit, you spend two days in a public health setting observing occupational therapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply foundational knowledge of the psychometric properties of occupational therapy assessment and measures.
Reflect upon the occupational therapy role in a professional practice setting and your professional behaviour, professional reasoning, and communication as a healthcare professional student.
Locate, retrieve, and apply credible resources and research evidence that underpin core occupational therapy practice principles.
Describe and apply theoretical concepts, models, and frameworks that can guide occupational therapy professional practice.
Explain and apply the professional reasoning processes used in occupational therapy practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral presentation (20 minutes total (10 mins presentation and 10 mins questions)

workload_hours: Two hours of self-directed learning per week, two hours of tutorial/practicum per week, two hours of workshops (three weeks of the semester), six hours of private study per week. Two-hour seminar in Week 1. Two-day observation practice education placement at a local public health network (15 hours)

title: Psychology for occupational therapy
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn about psychological theory relevant to the practice of occupational therapy, such as sensation and perception, cognition, emotion, personality, mental disorders, and social psychology. You will explore the application of these theories to occupational therapy practice through real world case studies. In this application, you will learn and apply strategies for effective teamwork, learning, and the communication of theories in different formats.
learning_outcomes: Apply strategies for effective teamwork and learning in professional practice.
Apply psychological theories, concepts and perspectives to real world scenarios.
Communicate effectively psychological theories, concepts and perspectives in multiple formats.
Identify and discuss key psychological theories, concepts, and perspectives applicable to human health and wellbeing.
Explain how psychological theory can be applied in occupational therapy practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group case study (1,500 words + 10 min presentation)
Class tests x 3 (45 minutes per test)

workload_hours: 2.5 hours of tutorial/workshop, 2 hours of online student learning activities (lectures & associated), plus 7.5 hours of self-directed study per week.

title: Human occupation and development
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: You will learn about the principles and mechanisms underlying the relationship between persons, their environments and occupations; and how it relates to human health and wellbeing. The concept of occupation will be described, and how people shape and are shaped by their engagement in occupation and their environmental context across the lifespan. This unit will describe how individuals change and develop as they age, exploring the occupational processes inherent in human development, and in doing so examining the progressive cognitive, physical, emotional, behavioural, psychosocial and occupational changes that occur with age. You will engage in experiential exercises to support and reinforce their learning of human occupation and life-stage development concepts, including participation in a community-based volunteering experience.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective presentation skills in written, visual and verbal modes
Describe and explain classifications of human occupation, and how the interaction of person-environment-occupation relates to health and wellbeing
Locate, retrieve and use resources to identify the relationship between persons, their environments and occupations and key occupational science concepts relevant for practice
Identify data collection methods, collect and analyse data on the occupational performance of self and others
Describe observations and critique these in relation to developmental theories about typical childhood occupations
Articulate and contrast contemporary developmental lifespan concepts, theories and research
Examine issues relevant to a health professional as well as reflect upon work completed as a team after participation in a community-based volunteering experience
Identify and discuss the physical, cognitive, emotional, behavioural, social and occupational aspects of development across the lifespan, and the influence on development of external factors
incompatibilities: OCC1032: Occupational development across the lifespan

assessment_tasks.task_name: Participation in practice based education - reflective journal (500 words) (Pass/Fail)
Individual Written Exam (2 hours and 10 minutes)

workload_hours: Academic: 8 hours of teacher directed study per week, composed of 2 hours of seminars (24 hours for teaching period), 2 hours online activities and 4 hours of tutorials (48 hours for teaching period),12 hours of self-directed study per week. Total per week = 20 hours (240 hours for teaching period) Practice education placement experience: You will complete 45 hours of practice education placement experience over the course of the semester. Four (4) hours per week of community placement has been calculated in the unit workload requirement. You will be required to travel locally to the community-based organisation to complete your placement hours. Community placement counts towards the minimum 1,000 hours of placement experience that is a requirement for student graduation and course accreditation (OT Council). Total per week: 24 hours per week

title: Foundation clinical sciences for occupational therapy
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit builds on foundation anatomy and physiology units BMA1901 and BMA1902 and aims to provide you with an understanding of functional anatomy and pathophysiology to inform the practice of Occupational Therapy. The unit provides advanced study of functional musculoskeletal anatomy, functional brain and spinal cord anatomy. The unit includes an introduction to neurochemistry and pharmacology and the pathophysiology of cerebrovascular accidents and traumatic brain, spinal and nerve injury. The function of the central nervous system is studied in relation to cognition and behaviour, including age-related changes, memory, altered states such as sleep, and the neurobiology of mental illness, in particular, autism and schizophrenia. You will learn through lectures and workshops with an emphasis on case-cased learning. Assessment includes a written and practical exam, peer-review and quizzes.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the basic neurochemistry, use and action of different classes of psychoactive drugs and explain the potential issues relating to occupational therapy.
Evaluate body functions, body structures and related clinical conditions and the applications to occupational performance challenges for clients of occupational therapy.
Describe the musculoskeletal anatomy related to movement and apply anatomical principles to determine function and common pathology
Discuss the pathophysiology and clinical consequences of stroke and traumatic brain, spinal and nerve injury;
Explain the mechanisms and consequences of mental/psychosocial, physical and social capacities of humans across the lifespan.
Explain the functions and structure of the nervous system in relation to cognition, affect, memory formation and motor control.
prerequisites: OCC2014: Occupational performance, capabilities and components
workload_hours: 2 hours per week contact time in weeks 1 to 3, and 1 hour per week subsequently. 6 to 10 hours private study including reviewing online resources and preparing for class presentations Seminars: 2 hours recorded online Laboratory classes: 2 hours, weeks 1 to 3 Workshops: 1 hour

title: Occupational performance, capabilities and components
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: The unit uses an integrated scenario/case-based learning approach. You are introduced to mechanisms and consequences of problems related to mental, sensory, cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological and biomechanical capacities that underpin occupational engagement and occupational performance. You integrate this knowledge into occupational therapy and related theories/models of practice. They develop clinical questions, and acquire knowledge and skills from the process of describing and evaluating occupational performance, and assessing occupational engagement/performance. You will explore different contexts in which participation in occupation takes place.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the rights of consumers and carers and integrate their lived experience of health needs into service planning and delivery
Locate, retrieve and use resources to inform decision making about health and occupational issues.
Apply critical appraisal, critical reasoning and critical thinking skills to occupational therapy scenario-based learning
Apply key theoretical models of human occupation to client-centred occupational therapy assessment, and goal setting
Clearly articulate to clients the specialist contribution of occupational therapy to health service intervention
Describe occupational justice issues in the allocation and distribution of resources within services
Appraise occupational therapy assessment tools and apply them in clinical contexts to evaluate occupational performance and occupational engagement
Describe and apply the principles of occupational analysis and grading and adaptation of occupations to a therapy situation

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written/oral examination (Part 1- 2 hrs with 10 mins reading Part 2-10 mins oral presentation)
Scenario-based occupational analysis assessment (2 x 5 mins oral presentations)
2 x 10 minute case scenario oral presentations
Written examination (2 hours with 10 mins reading time)

workload_hours: On campus: Total 12 hours scheduled per week. This includes: 6 hours Scenario Based Learning (SBL) tutorials 2 hours lecture/on-line 4 hours practicum. Off campus: 12 hours self-directed study per week. This time will involve research and preparation required for SBLs, pre-readings and tasks for practicum and SBLs.

title: Enabling occupation: Performance challenges 1A
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is the first unit of the occupational therapy intervention units. It comprises integrated case-based learning, skills-based learning, theories and evidence-based practice with participation in practice education placement to consolidate application of knowledge into practice. You will apply and critique the principles of assessment and intervention for clients with problems related to capacities to engage in activities, occupations, and participation in community life. Intervention principles will also incorporate environmental supports and barriers (advocacy, organisational change, environmental adaptation), and evidence-based practice. You will begin to develop appropriate intervention plans for clients based on assessment findings and evidence. Building on the skills acquired in OCC2013, you will further develop their professional competencies in professional behaviour, information gathering, communication with clients and co-workers, documentation, time-management, occupational therapy assessment, intervention and evaluation. You will participate in two weeks (four days per week) of practice education placement to develop these competencies. You will be provided with feedback and guided to reflect on and in practice within both academic and clinical contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective use of search strategies to identify and apply evidence-based practice for typical occupational therapy scenarios.
Describe common musculoskeletal, medical, surgical, neurological, mental and psychosocial disease processes relevant to clients of occupational therapy in the context of their occupational sequelae;
Select, measure, prescribe and use appropriate assistive equipment to create recommendations for increased occupational participation and performance in typical client scenarios;

Apply the Canadian Model of Occupational Performance and Engagement (CMOP-E) and the Canadian Practice Process Framework (CPPF) to typical occupational therapy practice scenarios addressing different areas of practice;
Integrate evidence-based practice with a client-centred approach to recommend relevant occupational therapy intervention strategies and services;
Apply and explain typical occupational therapy theories, intervention strategies, methods and modalities used with clients of occupational therapy;
Demonstrate effective communication skills to provide relevant, concise and comprehensive written and oral reports based on information gathered from assessments, observations and interviews;
Apply principles of orthotic fabrication to design, manufacture and critique orthoses;
Implement appropriate professional behaviour in both academic and practice education environments with health care team members, consumers, carers, practice education supervisors, and academic staff.
Demonstrate abilities to apply knowledge and skills for information gathering, evaluation, goal setting and intervention planning related to occupational therapy practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: One x 1.5 hours short answers and MCQ BMA exam
One x 1.5 hours short answer and MCQ OT theory exam
Critical evaluation of an orthosis (1,000 words and submission of orthosis)
Practice education workbook & case presentation (3,000 words)10 minutes oral presentation
2 x case scenario oral presentations (8 minutes each)

workload_hours: This unit will run for 10 weeks of academic teaching, followed by one week Swot Vac, one week of exams and four weeks of practice education placement. The workload demand is 10-15 hours contact time . 5.5 hours Scenario Based Learning (SBL) tutorials 4 to 6 hours seminars/online lecture 3 to 4 hours workshops/ tutorials (practical) Private study: 10 - 14 hours of self-directed study per week. This time will involve research and preparation for SBLs, reveiwing prescribed readings and completing preparatory tasks for practicums and workshops. Practice education placement: 7 days (or equivalent)

title: Introduction to occupational therapy professional practice
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will prepare you for occupational therapy professional practice and includes applying clinical reasoning in relation to the practice activities you will engage in. You will apply theoretical knowledge to the practice environment, learn to gather relevant client information, demonstrate client-centred practice, and basic documentation skills (including writing assessment reports, progress notes, and intervention goals and objectives). You will gain experience in critiquing assessment tools that occupational therapists use in a practice. You will also complete seven days (or equivalent) of practice education placement to develop self-management skills; communication skills with clients, co-workers, and other key stakeholders; information gathering and documentation skills; ability to work in a team; and client centred and reflective practice skills. You will be provided with feedback and guided to reflect on and in practice within both academic and clinical contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate abilities to apply knowledge and skills for information gathering, evaluation, goal setting, professional documentation, and planning, relevant to occupational therapy assessment.
Apply key human occupation theoretical models and frameworks relevant to occupational therapy practice and daily living environments.
Apply knowledge and principles of accessible environments relevant to home environment evaluation, designing technical drawings, and providing recommendations for home modifications.
Select, administer, appraise, and critique assessment tools and assessment methods used in occupational therapy practice.
Explain the occupational therapy role relevant to different professional practice settings and key stakeholders.
Apply the principles of client-centred practice, the clinical reasoning process, and self-reflective practice, to occupational therapy practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Home assessment report (1,500 words and sketch and technical drawing)
Portfolio (Essay-1,000 words; video demonstration; oral presentation-8 mins in pairs)

workload_hours: 12 hours of study per week comprising: 6 - 8 hours of online seminars, online activities, and on-campus tutorials; and 4 -6 hours of self-directed study Practice education placement: 7 days (or equivalent).

title: Skills for evidence-based practice in occupational therapy
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an overview of the skills necessary to critique and evaluate the usefulness, relevance and quality of research evidence related to occupational therapy professional practice. Components of evidence-based practice will be introduced related to occupational therapy. Quantitative and qualitative research methodology approaches that underpin evidence-based practice will also be introduced. You will be guided through the process of how to ask clinically relevant questions, search for evidence, and critically appraise published research studies. The Monash Occupational Therapy Research Evidence Critique Form (MOTRECF) for both quantitative and qualitative studies will be used to evaluate the relevant evidence. The process used to complete a critically appraised paper (CAP) will also be introduced. This will provide the foundation for you to integrate clinically relevant evidence into your daily professional practice as well as providing you with the skills required for analysing the issues dealt with in the scenario-based learning context used in OCC2020, OCC3031, and OCC3052.
learning_outcomes: Apply and implement skills related to gathering and interpreting evidence from empirical literature to support professional and clinical practice;
Describe, apply and evaluate qualitative research methodologies and methods;
Describe and apply knowledge of quantitative and qualitative research paradigms relevant to occupational therapy practice;
Apply basic parametric and non-parametric statistics;
Discuss ethical issues and practices related to research;
Evaluate and apply general measurement concepts: levels of measurement, reliability, validity;
Explain the role of theory in occupational therapy research;
Apply and integrate principles outlined in the Monash Occupational Therapy Research Evidence Critique Form (MOTRECF) related to quantitative studies and qualitative studies to critique evidence.
Recognise the relevance of research in occupational therapy practice;
prerequisites: OCC2013: Introduction to occupational therapy professional practice
OCC2014: Occupational performance, capabilities and components
workload_hours: Lecture component: 3 hours per week, Tutorial/Practicum component: 3 hours per week, Private study: 4 hours per week.

title: Enabling occupation: Performance challenges 1B
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is the second unit of the occupational therapy intervention units. It comprises 10 weeks of integrated scenario-based learning.
