In the process, there will be opportunities to explore the complex relationships between humans, development, and the natural environment, and assess the potential for sustainable, inclusive approaches to conservation and governance that prioritize the needs of local communities and the environment.
learning_outcomes: Apply key theoretical concepts, such as Arnstein's Ladder of Empowerment, to critically analyse the empowerment and participation of local communities in development processes, and assess the different levels of participation and decision-making power that communities have in shaping their own socioeconomic and environmental future.

Explore various solutions, such as the creation and management of a community-conserved area (CCA) as a shared platform for stakeholders to come together, and assess the potential benefits, challenges, and implications of such an approach for biodiversity conservation, livelihoods, and inclusive governance, based on existing case studies and best practices;
Evaluate the concepts of political ecology, including power relations, social inequalities, and governance dynamics, and their impacts on both the environment and rural, marginalized communities;

Illustrate an understanding of the role and impact of humans and development on the natural environment by exploring traditional livelihoods, the concept of local knowledge, and how local communities work to preserve the environment and local species for their long-term sustainability;
workload_hours: Minimum total expected workload to achieve the learning outcomes for this unit is 144 hours per semester comprising a mixture of scheduled learning activities (100 hours) and independent study (44 hours). Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher directed learning, peer directed learning and online engagement.

title: Laboratory and workplace management
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed to introduce intending scientists to the principles of laboratory and workplace management and their obligations as experts and supervisors. It will cover legislation and the responsibilities of both employers and employees in issues such as occupational health and safety; handling of dangerous goods and the analysis, treatment and disposal of hazardous materials. Emphasis will be placed on the assessment and management of these issues in a laboratory and workplace environment. The subject will be taught by programmed learning material and practical work consisting of assessment and discussion of case studies and workplace excursions.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of chemistry, biology, microbiology and physical science to the treatment of hazardous materials;
Describe their obligations under the Occupational Health and Safety Act and related legislation;
Outline their legislated obligations in recycling and disposal of hazardous materials;
Recommend procedures for the analysis and treatment of hazardous wastes before disposal to the environment.
Discuss selected issues in managing a scientific laboratory;
Undertake a risk assessment and recommend safe working procedures;
Discuss the effects of waste materials on the environment;
Recognise hazards associated with chemical and biological materials, instruments and ionising radiation and the risks they impose;
workload_hours: Two 1-hour lectures; One 2-hour tutorial and Eight hours of independent study per week

title: Impact through science 3B
syllabus_overview: Impact through science 3B provides the opportunity for you to further cultivate your persuasive communication, leadership and entrepreneurial skills through a self-directed and real-world project. The aim of this extended project is for you to develop a creative solution enabling the application of scientific research to the needs of society. You will negotiate a project scope with a research scientist within the Science Faculty that directly draws upon your research, meets the aims of the Bachelor of Science - Global Challenges (Honours) and falls under one of three project themes: 1) A new product or service utilising the scientific research; 2) Closing the gap between science and policy/politics; 3) Science communication to the general public. During the course of this unit you will also be required to submit your final internship project plans.
learning_outcomes: Apply project management skills to develop, implement and deliver the specified project.
Articulate the importance of disruptive and innovative thinking to achieve impact through science.
Demonstrate critical thinking and persuasive communication through written reports and oral presentation.
Undertake independent research to demonstrate an understanding of the current scientific, social, corporate and/or political contexts of the projects.
Refine teamwork capabilities and identify areas for improvement.
workload_hours: This unit requires on average three/four hours of scheduled activities per week. Scheduled activities may include a combination of teacher directed learning, peer directed learning and online engagement. Additional requirements for at least eight hours of independent work including project work, meeting with the unit coordinator and other research activities are required.

title: Science internship
syllabus_overview: The internship gives you the opportunity to apply your university learning to the workplace, providing you with experience in tailoring their academic-based learning to the needs of an industry-based partner, and to network with potential employers. This will prepare you for work or professional practice by integrating theoretical knowledge with practice. You will learn about the process of applying for employment and good workplace practice. The internship will generally be over the summer break and commence in December. It can be taken any time after the completion of level two.
learning_outcomes: Understand the requirements of working with others in a position of responsibility;
Set personal goals and to pursue these goals in a manner appropriate to the workplace.
Work effectively as a member of a team through well-developed skills in job planning, time management, problem solving, critical thinking and the organisation of work;
Recognise OHS issues and demonstrate application of safe practices in a workplace environment;
Develop effective and appropriate communication skills;
Illustrate a positive contribution to the organisation;
Apply the knowledge and skills acquired during their academic studies to the practical requirements of the workplace;
workload_hours: Three hour workshop prior to internship Minimum eight weeks of placement One-hour of private study per week

title: Science internship
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will undertake a science based internship of three full-time weeks (or part-time equivalent hours), where you will put into practice the knowledge and skills developed in your course. The internship experience will give you hands-on, real world exposure to the workplace environment and will supplement your academic growth to develop your graduate attributes and employability skills. You will work with a host supervisor to establish professional objectives, a project plan, and to receive feedback on your progress. The internship will help you develop self-awareness of your ability to meet stated objectives and areas in need of improvement. A pre-placement workshop run by the Industry Engagement team will support your preparation for the placement and develop an understanding of science-based professions, the work culture, and the skills and attributes required for the workplace. Bespoke workshops during your internship will enhance your personal and professional brand. You have two options to source your internship. With the approval of the Unit Coordinator and the Industry Engagement team, you can source your own internship host. Alternatively, you can apply for a Monash Sourced placement, which is via a competitive process. *Note: Internships for students enrolled in the Winter semester are self-sourced only
learning_outcomes: Actively seek out and act upon constructive feedback;
Analyse professional skills through critical reflective practice and create a plan to improve an under-developed skill in the context of work-readiness;
Demonstrate and convey the knowledge, skills and attributes required for the professional workplace in a relevant science or applied science setting;
Create a project-related output and communicate effectively using oral, written and visual forms to peers, academics and placement supervisors.
Review and reflect on the insights gained from the immersion in a professional setting, and the impact of this experience on career development;
workload_hours: One 2-hour pre-placement induction and Four 2-hour workshops across the semester plus an Industry placement of three full-time weeks (or part-time equivalent hours). The exact timing and distribution of hours for individual placements will be determined by negotiation between student and host.

title: Science internship (Extended)
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will undertake a science internship of six full-time weeks (or part-time equivalent hours), where you will put into practice the knowledge and skills developed in your course. The internship experience will give you hands-on, real world exposure to the workplace environment and will supplement your academic growth to develop your graduate attributes and employability skills. The internship will help you develop self-awareness of your ability to meet stated objectives and areas in need of improvement. A pre-placement workshop run by the Industry Engagement team will support your preparation for the placement and develop an understanding of science-based professions, the work culture, and the skills and attributes required for the workplace. Bespoke workshops during your internship will enhance your personal and professional brand. You have two options to source your internship. With the approval of the Unit Coordinator and the Industry Engagement team, you can source your own internship host. Alternatively, you can apply for a Monash Sourced placement, which is a competitive process.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attributes required for the professional workplace in a relevant science or applied science setting;
Review and reflect on the insights gained from the immersion in a professional setting, and the impact of this experience on career development;
Analyse professional skills through critical reflective practice and create a plan to improve an under-developed skill in the context of work-readiness and career planning;
Actively seek out and act upon constructive feedback;
Create a deliverable and communicate effectively using oral, written and visual forms to peers, academics and placement supervisors.
workload_hours: One 2-hour pre-placement induction; Seven 2-hour workshops across the semester; Industry placement: of of six full-time weeks (or part-time equivalent hours). The exact timing and distribution of hours for individual placements will be determined by negotiation between student and host.

title: Science in action research project
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an opportunity for you to undertake an individual research project in a discipline relating to a major area of study, that is conducted with a supervisor. You will develop skills in critical literature review, experimental design, data analysis, and report writing. You must maintain regular contact with supervisor(s) and subject coordinator. The experience gained in the unit will serve as training for postgraduate or professional research.
learning_outcomes: Conduct independent research, including defining research questions and developing research methodology;
Analyse and explain the broader scientific and social aspects of research in their chosen field;
Manage time and the project with autonomy and efficiency, and communicate effectively with relevant stakeholders;
Generate, manipulate, and interpret data relevant to the discipline;
Effectively present the research project orally, graphically and in written form.
Review and critically evaluate the scientific literature within the discipline;
workload_hours: Approximately 12 hours per week

title: Career skills for scientists
syllabus_overview: This unit prepares you to apply for graduate level employment. It uses work-related activities to develop and enhance your transferable skills, and focusses on essential career planning. Commercial awareness is the umbrella theme of the unit due to its critical importance in the workplace. You will explore aspects such as the intellectual property landscape, budgeting, regulation, quality control, marketing strategy, and the business environment through creative problem-solving activities. The unit also focuses on other important skills for graduate employment, including communication, leadership, collaboration, problem-solving and critical thinking. You will audit your key employability skills, reflect on ongoing development and keep a record of your self-evaluation so you can better articulate your skills to potential employers. The unit also offers opportunities to explore various career pathways, job search strategies, and prepare an effective job application that includes a resume, cover letter and response to selection criteria.
learning_outcomes: Develop a sense of inclusivity and professionalism in the workplace.
Apply the principles of networking and self-promotion and reflect on their impact in a professional context;
Recognise and develop skills that will be valuable in the workplace;
Articulate your range of scientific and professional skills through preparation of a job application;
Self-evaluate and reflect on your employment readiness with respect to the key employability skills;
Present clear evidence of how your skills and experience can benefit potential employers;
workload_hours: SEMESTER 1 Eight 2-hour workshop and 128 hours of private/independent study WINTER / SUMMER Four 4-hour workshops and 128 hours of private/independent study

title: Science honours project
syllabus_overview: You will undertake a supervised research project in an area of science, and present the results in a seminar.
learning_outcomes: Be able to complete and analyse a set of laboratory-based, computer-based, theoretical or other appropriate studies;
Have demonstrated the capability to perform a variety of scientific procedures and techniques that are essential to the satisfactory completion and reporting of a research project;
Demonstrate communication skills in both oral and written presentations, including the ability to write and present scientific work in a potentially publishable way;
Critically review the scientific literature in their specialist area of study;
Have acquired a range of technical skills and attitudes appropriate to their specialist area of study;
Understand the processes involved in the design, development and implementation of a relevant research project;
Be proficient in computer based data acquisition (where appropriate), critical analysis of results, appropriate presentation, and scientific word processing;

title: Impact through science 4A: Research
syllabus_overview: By working with industry and/or academic partners you will complete an independent research project. You will gain authentic industry experience and an applied understanding of the nature of the industry and stakeholder needs. This unit will develop your theoretical understanding of your industry research challenge. You will immerse yourself in the literature surrounding your chosen field of research, develop a research strategy, demonstrate understanding of your chosen topic, and generate industry-relevant data. You will present the results in an individual written thesis. The unit will prepare you for the development of the project plan and commencement of the group based Challenge project in SCI4502 (semester 2).
learning_outcomes: Integrate research into a professional report that articulates the problem and possible solutions and shows critical thinking and persuasive communication;
Undertake and interpret independent research to demonstrate a critical and analytical understanding of the current scientific, social, corporate and/or political contexts of the project;
Execute a stakeholder analysis and appraise a range of needs to evaluate and illustrate the problem;
Use persuasive presentation skills to articulate the problem and possible solutions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Module 1 - Organisational structure, project design and professional skills

workload_hours: 36 hours of study per week comprised of independent research, meetings, and workshops. This unit delivers 50% of the full-time fourth-year program for the BSc Advanced - Global Challenges (Honours). Scheduled activities will include a combination of face-to-face classes, purpose developed online modules, research colloquia, seminars, and meetings with your Industry and academic supervisors. The unit includes two intensive weeks of induction in the first two weeks of February.

title: Impact through science 4B: Professional practice
syllabus_overview: As a team, you will collaboratively design and develop solutions to your industry partner’s real-world problem. You will gain exposure to professional practice and build industry partner relationships. This unit will build your practical skills in project design and management, negotiation, workplace communication and innovation. You will generate industry-relevant data and design solutions to the challenges presented by your industry partner, You will present your findings in a group as a written Challenge project report and oral defence.
learning_outcomes: Apply project management skills to identify a feasible scope, timeline and resources needed to execute the project;
Produce innovative and feasible solution(s) to a defined problem that utilises evidence and knowledge of the industry;
Collaboratively participate in the design, development and implementation of a project to a high standard of professionalism;
Articulate your solution(s) by using persuasive professional communication and presentation skills.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Challenge project – oral presentation and defence
Project plan oral presentation to external partners

workload_hours: Your workload is an average of 36 hours of study per week comprised of independent research, meetings, and workshops. This unit delivers 50% of the full-time fourth-year program for the BSc Advanced - Global Challenges (Honours). Scheduled activities will include a combination of face-to-face classes, purpose developed online modules, research colloquia, seminars, and meetings with your Industry and Academic supervisors. The unit includes two intensive weeks of induction in the first two weeks of February.

title: Master work integrated learning project
faculty: School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment
syllabus_overview: The unit provides students, who fulfil the academic requirements, with an opportunity to undertake a project defined by a host organisation with the approval of the unit coordinator. The placement may be an affiliated arrangement where a consultancy or research project is carried out in association with the company and physical location at the company is not required, or a simulated industrial environment hosted on campus. Host organisations may be from a diverse range of industries and sectors, including government departments, private industry and not-for-profit organisations. You will present the project findings to the host organisation in the format specified by the host organisation, such as a consultation paper, report, commentary, manual, submission or speech. The host organisation provides field supervision, and the faculty provides academic supervision.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with others on a project in a workplace setting;
Plan, conduct and reflect upon a professional project with a degree of independence and accountability;
Communicate clearly and effectively to the intended audience on technical and non-technical aspects;
Exercise critical thinking and professional judgment in developing new understandings;
Demonstrate professional conduct and integrity in a workplace environment.
Apply broad discipline knowledge to find solutions to complex problems;
workload_hours: The minimum expected workload for the unit is 288 hours over the course of one semester. This mostly comprises of project work, and also includes 6 hours of scheduled workshops, preparation of assessments, and presenting your oral assessment.

title: Material transformations: Ceramics
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This unit will engage with the practice of working with clay based processes and will look at current exhibitions of contemporary artists that employ ceramics in their practices. You will explore the potential of clay in forming objects, replicating multiples, as well different firing and finishing techniques. This unit will also address the environmental considerations of working with clay. The unit will focus on the development of sculptural and object based technologies specific to the formed object. You will be encouraged to explore various traditional as well as contemporary processes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate abilities to safely and effectively use specialist material processes and equipment to generate outcomes.
Investigate, critically analyse and develop the expressive and forming potential of clay-based processes and techniques;
Demonstrate an awareness of the environmental impact of the production of clay-based objects;
Produce new work achieved through exploring various clay-based processes and techniques;
Explore and analyse various cultural and material values of clay-based objects;
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 12 hours per week including 4 contact hours plus 8 hours of independent study and studio practice.

title: Material transformations: Glass and sculptural forming
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to contemporary thinking about working with materials, the unique properties of specific material, like glass, and the potential for material transformation in creative practices. The unit will focus on the development of processes specific to the cast object, including a consideration of the readymade or found object. Drawing on design and fine art histories and methodologies you will explore a range of processes using glass and other materials used in contemporary sculpture. You are encouraged to investigate traditional as well as contemporary materials.
learning_outcomes: Develop studio processes that generate creative research in various sculptural materials;
Demonstrate abilities to safely and effectively use specialist material processes and equipment to generate outcomes.
Demonstrate an understanding of material propositions appropriate to the concepts under investigation;
Critically reflect on the place of the design and sculptural object in various material expressions in the fields of contemporary creative practice art, nationally and internationally;
Apply conceptual and material understanding of different casting, forming and finishing processes in the context of contemporary object and sculptural production;
Position and articulate the aesthetic, theoretical and historical context of your creative practice;
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 12 hours per week including 4 contact hours plus 8 hours of independent study and studio practice.

title: Spatial design studio 2
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will engage with experiential and functional qualities of space. Two projects will explore the key concept of inhabitation for both human and non-human beings. You will be introduced to design methods such as site analysis, observation, conceptual model making, and iterative design processes. You will develop representation and communication skills through a combination of digital and hand-based drawing and modelling techniques, as well as verbal presentations.
learning_outcomes: Create detailed 2D and 3D spatial representations using computer-aided design software to communicate design intentions, while engaging with concepts and scales of space, including experiential aspects for both human and non-human beings;
Demonstrate foundational knowledge of spatial design principles and methods, including site analysis, observation, and conceptual modelling, to inform design proposals;
Engage with peers and participate in groups providing constructive feedback to others clearly communicating your design ideas and outcomes;
Develop a design proposal that responds to a project brief, adapting solutions to meet contextual and audience needs;
Consider aesthetic, functional, sustainable, and programmatic aspects in design outcomes, demonstrating a commitment to ethical and responsible spatial practices;
Document and reflect on the design proposal process, using diverse media and iterative practices to assess design development.
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 24 hours per week including 6 contact hours plus 18 hours of independent study.

title: Spatial design studio 3
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will engage with notions of change as a key consideration for spatial practice. Two fundamental modules will be explored: the development of design as a process of discovery, connecting introductory research concepts; and the assembly of materials in spatial practice. In the first module you will focus on the temporal aspects of space, and the connection of design ideas, materials, and experiences to change and transformation. In the second module services within inhabited environments will be introduced, and explored by you through focused observation and project work.
learning_outcomes: Examine, reflect and respond to aesthetic, functional, sustainable, and programmatic aspects in the development of a design proposal;
Collaborate in diverse teams by exchanging ideas and feedback with peers and considering stakeholder perspectives, while effectively presenting outcomes in a clear and engaging manner;
Apply exploratory strategies within an iterative design process, using time-based representation techniques to develop and communicate design schemes;
Integrate temporal elements, material qualities, and user experience through iterative experimentation, acting on feedback to develop cohesive and context-sensitive design outcomes;

Document and reflect on each stage of the design proposal process, incorporating diverse media and iterative practices to enhance design development and engage in self-reflection to deepen your understanding of your design practice.
Explain key temporal concepts and their relevance to spatial design, and identify appropriate materials and their structural qualities to support design intentions;
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 24 hours per week including 6 contact hours plus 18 hours of independent study.

title: Spatial design studio 4
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will focus on spatial advocacy and social contexts through an empathetic and situated approach. You will explore the ways spatial design practice relates to and influences justice, resilience, and equity through examining critical social, political, economic, and environmental issues. You will develop your own ways of working with materials and construction in a manner that supports these ideas, and build competency in designing experiences and in effective communication of conceptual thinking that expands beyond utilitarian, problem-solving design. You will learn to collaborate empathetically with experts, communities, and stakeholders within your project area.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate contemporary issues related to spatial design, acting on feedback to deepen your critique and enhance your understanding;

Develop methods for initiating, documenting, refining, and communicating a design project, adapting strategies to support the design process, while engaging in self-reflection to identify areas for growth and challenges within your practice.
Identify and explain the impact of social, political, economic, and environmental issues on spatial design practices;

Collaborate with experts and stakeholders to analyse and address contemporary issues in spatial design, focusing on social justice and equity, while clearly articulating and communicating solutions and design outcomes;
Conduct research on new materials and construction appropriate for concept;
Develop and articulate strong conceptual ideas that emphasise justice, resilience, and equity in design practice;
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 24 hours per week including 6 contact hours plus 18 hours of independent study.

title: Spatial design studio 5
school: Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this final studio unit, you will develop speculative designs that reimagine the spaces we inhabit in the future. Building on skills developed in previous studios, you will develop your own design speculation in response to one of the focused studio themes. Your project will require you to demonstrate advanced research skills as you engage with complex issues around changing environmental, societal, and cultural landscapes in relation to spatial practice. You will develop your own methods of initiating, managing, developing, documenting and communicating your project.
learning_outcomes: Develop advanced methods for initiating, managing, documenting, refining, and communicating a design project, adapting strategies to support the design process, while engaging in self-reflection to address challenges and promote personal growth within your practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of the potential role of a spatial designer, and build your own design practice;
Investigate and critique complex issues related to spatial design, synthesising your research into a design proposal and acting on feedback to refine and strengthen your solution;
Initiate your own project, build design briefs, and document the resolution of competing needs during the development of a design proposal with increasing independence;
Articulate advanced conceptual ideas that engage with justice, resilience, and equity, demonstrating the ability to address complex challenges within spatial design practice;

Contribute meaningfully to your learning community by collaborating with peers, experts, and stakeholders to address real-world challenges, demonstrating your understanding of the spatial designer's role and effectively communicating project outcomes to diverse audiences;
prerequisites: OHS1000: Introduction to art and design health and safety
workload_hours: 24 hours per week including 6 contact hours plus 18 hours of independent study.

title: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to the scientific and technical principles of diagnostic ultrasound. You will learn how to apply ultrasound physics to obtain high-quality diagnostic images, understand and compare different ultrasound modes, and optimise machine settings for clinical use. Doppler imaging and its clinical applications are explored, along with safety considerations and the potential bioeffects of ultrasound. In this unit you will develops skills in quality assurance, image artefact recognition, and effective communication of ultrasound knowledge to patients, peers, and other healthcare professionals.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of advanced imaging techniques, contrast agents, and evolving ultrasound technologies to optimise diagnostic imaging.
Evaluate ultrasound modes and machine parameters to optimise instrumentation and produce high-quality diagnostic images.
Apply the principles of ultrasound physics to evaluate and optimise image quality for accurate diagnostic interpretation.
Reflect on personal motivations and experiences to shape professional identity, ethical practice, and pateint-centred care.
Justify how Doppler imaging is applied in clinical practice.
Interpret the potential bioeffects of medical ultrasound to ensure safe clinical practice.
workload_hours: Applied Sessions: 2 hours per week (2 x 12 weeks = 24) Tutorials: 2 hours per semester. Teaching is all online.

title: Embryology, anatomy and pathophysiology
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides a detailed study of embryology, anatomy, and physiology across key body systems, including the central nervous, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, vascular, musculoskeletal, and hepatobiliary systems. You will explore structure-function relationships and apply this knowledge to recognise normal and abnormal anatomical and physiological presentations. In this unit you will develop foundational ultrasound skills, enabling you to evaluate findings accurately, support safe, evidence-based diagnostic practice, and communicate results effectively within the healthcare team.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of anatomical movement, function, and pathology to support clinical evaluation and diagnosis.
Evaluate ultrasound findings to differentiate pathological presentations in the support of clinical decisions.
Integrate principles of embryological development and physiology to evaluate body systems.
Apply foundational image recognition skills to communicate findings to the broader healthcare team.
Assess clinical information to enable safe, evidence-based diagnostic ultrasound practice.
Analyse structure-function relationships to explain abnormal anatomical presentations.
workload_hours: Applied Sessions: 2 hours per week (2 x 12 weeks = 24 hours) Tutorials: 2 hours per semester

title: Ultrasound research
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit develops advanced research skills in medical ultrasound, equipping you to critically evaluate literature, identify research questions, and design and conduct coherent research projects. You will explore practical, technical, and ethical considerations in research, apply appropriate methodologies, and analyse findings to generate new knowledge. The unit also fosters professional communication, self-management, and reflective practice, enabling you to translate critical and creative thinking into evidence-based clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise self-management and reflective practice, to apply critical and ethical thinking to research decisions.
Evaluate research methodologies to investigate clinical questions and generate new knowledge.
Implement the practical, technical, and managerial aspects of designing and conducting a research project.
Communicate research findings effectively to professional and academic audiences.
Evaluate ethical considerations in research and manage the process of obtaining Ethics Approval.
Formulate research problems in medical ultrasound and design coherent research plans to address specific questions.
Appraise the validity and impact of medical literature to inform evidence-based clinical ultrasound practice.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation
SON5020: Sonographic professional skills and sonography of the breast and thyroid
SON5022: Sonographic imaging of the reproductive system
SON5024: Musculoskeletal, neonatal and paediatric sonography
SON5025: Sonographic vascular and postoperative imaging
SRH5003: Designing and conducting health research

title: Sonographic professional skills and sonography of the breast and thyroid
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces key principles of medical law, ethics, and professional practice, alongside culturally safe and inclusive approaches to address racism and bias in healthcare. You will develop advanced skills in performing thyroid and breast ultrasound examinations, interpreting normal and abnormal findings, and applying evidence-based knowledge to support accurate clinical decision-making. The unit also emphasises effective communication and collaboration with patients and multidisciplinary teams, and encourages reflection on professional growth to enhance clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and collaborate effectively with patients and multidisciplinary teams to deliver safe, patient-centred care.
Reflect on professional growth to enhance clinical excellence and advance thyroid and breast ultrasound practice.
Evaluate normal and abnormal thyroid and breast sonographic appearances to inform accurate clinical decision-making.
Apply advanced knowledge and skills when performing thyroid and breast ultrasound examinations in compliance with evidence-based practice.
Integrate the principles of medical law, ethics, and professionalism in ultrasound practice.
Apply culturally safe and inclusive practice to address racism, bias, and inequity in healthcare.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation
workload_hours: Applied Sessions: 2 x hours per week (2 x 12 weeks = 24 hours) Tutorials: 3 hours per semester Teaching is all online.

title: Sonographic abdominal imaging
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with comprehensive training in abdominal ultrasound, covering sonographic scanning methods and evidence-based protocols for abdominal and retroperitoneal organs and related vascular structures. You will develop advanced skills in image acquisition and interpretation, including recognition of normal anatomy, anatomical variants, and pathological findings, while adapting scanning approaches to suit the clinical question and patient presentation. The unit also emphasises the application of imaging findings to support clinical decision-making, effective communication with patients and healthcare teams, and reflective practice to enhance professional competence.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on clinical experiences and learning to enhance professional competence.
Interpret and evaluate normal and abnormal abdominal sonographic appearances to support clinical decision-making.
Integrate safe and effective scanning techniques to achieve high-quality abdominal imaging.
Communicate and collaborate with patients and healthcare professionals to support patient-centred care in ultrasound practice.
Apply evidence based abdominal ultrasound protocols to optimise the imaging outcomes.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation
workload_hours: Applied Sessions: 2 x hours per week (2 x 12 weeks = 24 hours) Tutorials: 2 hours per semester Teaching is all online.

title: Sonographic imaging of the reproductive system
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit you will develop advanced skills in reproductive system ultrasound, covering sonographic scanning methods, standard protocols, and interpretational skills for the female pelvis and male reproductive system. You will learn to recognise normal anatomy, anatomical variants, and pathological findings, and to adapt scanning approaches according to the clinical question and patient presentation. The unit also provides and opportunity for you to apply medico-legal and culturally safe practices during intimate examinations, integrating sonographic findings into clinical decision-making, effective communication with patients and healthcare teams, and reflective practice to enhance professional competence.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on clinical experiences and research-based activities to enhance professional competence.
Interpret and evaluate normal and abnormal reproductive sonographic appearances to support clinical decision-making.
Communicate and collaborate with patients and healthcare professionals to ensure patient-centred care.
Integrate advanced knowledge and skills when performing reproductive system ultrasound examinations.
Apply medico-legal and cultural safety principles to intimate reproductive ultrasound examinations.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation

title: Obstetric sonography
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop advanced obstetric ultrasound skills, focusing on evidence-based scanning methods and protocols throughout pregnancy, including the assessment of fetal growth, gestational age, and multiple pregnancies. You will gain competence in performing examinations, evaluating normal and abnormal findings, and interpreting sonographic appearances to inform clinical decision-making. During this unit you will communicate and collaborate with patients and multidisciplinary healthcare teams, applying ethical principles, and reflection on clinical and research-informed experiences to enhance professional competence and advance obstetric ultrasound practice.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with patients and multidisciplinary healthcare teams to support informed decision-making.
Analyse clinical experiences and research-informed activities to enhance professional competence and advance obstetric ultrasound practice.
Perform obstetric ultrasound examinations competently to achieve high-quality imaging.
Apply and justify evidence-based obstetric ultrasound protocols to optimise imaging outcomes.
Evaluate and interpret normal and abnormal obstetric sonographic appearances to inform clinical decision-making.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation

title: Musculoskeletal, neonatal and paediatric sonography
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop advanced skills in musculoskeletal and paediatric ultrasound, covering evidence-based scanning methods and protocols for the musculoskeletal system as well as the paediatric brain, hips, and abdomen. You will learn to interpret complex normal and abnormal findings, adapt scanning approaches to the clinical question and patient presentation, and apply principles of neonatal and paediatric care. The unit also provides an opportunity for you to apply effective communication and collaboration with patients and multidisciplinary healthcare teams, and encourages the integration of research evidence and clinical insights to support evidence-based ultrasound practice.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise research evidence and clinical insights to contribute to evidence-based practice.
Communicate and collaborate effectively with patients and multidisciplinary healthcare professionals in advanced ultrasound practice.
Apply advanced knowledge and skills when undertaking complex musculoskeletal and paediatric ultrasound examinations.
Evaluate normal and abnormal musculoskeletal and paediatric sonographic findings to support clinical decision-making.
Integrate advanced musculoskeletal and paediatric ultrasound protocols to optimise imaging quality and diagnostic accuracy.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation

title: Sonographic vascular and postoperative imaging
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop advanced skills in vascular ultrasound, focusing on evidence-based scanning methods, techniques, and protocols for the assessment of peripheral and central vessels. You will learn to interpret normal and abnormal vascular anatomy and physiology, including artefacts, stents, grafts, and post-transplant evaluations, to support accurate clinical decision-making. The unit also provides an opportunity for you to illustrate competent performance of vascular examinations, effective communication and collaboration with patients and healthcare teams, and reflection on clinical experiences to enhance professional practice in vascular sonography.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and collaborate with patients and healthcare professionals to support patient-centred care.
Synthesize clinical experiences and learning to enhance professional competence in vascular ultrasound practice.
Perform vascular ultrasound examinations competently using appropriate scanning techniques.
Evaluate normal and abnormal vascular sonographic appearances to support clinical decision-making
Justify evidence-based vascular ultrasound practice to achieve safe and accurate diagnostic outcomes.
prerequisites: SON4000: Physics of medical ultrasound and instrumentation

title: Professional identity in speech pathology
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit provides an essential foundation for your journey as a speech pathologist, focusing on the development of professional identity and the values that underpin contemporary practice. You will learn about the roles of speech pathologists in the management of communication and swallowing problems in diverse settings. You will explore the complex interplay between communication, mealtime practices, and personal and cultural identity. You will learn how the principles of social equity and justice can guide speech pathology practice. You will also develop skills in communication, collaboration and self-reflection. Your learning will be underpinned by the Speech Pathology Australia Professional Standards (2020) to help you identify yourself in this role.
learning_outcomes: Explore the work roles and professional skills, attributes and behaviours of Speech pathologists to identify oneself within this role.
Reflect on personal and professional perspectives to enhance self-awareness in relation to social equity, justice, diversity and inclusion.
Discuss the importance of communication and mealtime participation on personal and cultural identity formation.
Apply collaborative and evidence-based communication strategies in professional practice as a Speech pathologist.
Describe the role of speech pathologists in the management of communication and swallowing problems in diverse settings.
workload_hours: This unit will have 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week (4 hours of online learning activities (including a pre-recorded lecture), and 2 hours of on-campus workshops). Additionally, there are 6 hours of self-directed study per week, making the total workload 12 hours. Total workload per semester : 144 hours

title: Anatomy and physiology for speech, language and swallowing
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn the anatomical and physiological foundations essential for understanding speech, language, and swallowing functions required for speech pathology practice. You will study the structure and function of the respiratory, phonatory, articulatory, and nervous systems, with a focus on their relevance to communication and swallowing. This directly supports your ability to apply knowledge of key anatomical structures and physiological processes involved in speech pathology-related disorders and impairments. Emphasis is placed on the relationship between structure and function, and how impairments in these systems can affect communication and swallowing across the lifespan, aligning with your ability to examine the impact of disorders on activity and participation. Throughout the unit, you will be introduced to relevant clinical assessments and case-based learning that will help you discuss assessment approaches used in identifying speech pathology-related impairments. You will also begin to develop effective communication skills to support clients with anatomical and/or physiological concerns, laying the foundation for professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss relevant clinical assessments required in the identification of speech pathology-related disorders and impairments.
Demonstrate effective communication and self-reflexivity skills to support clients with anatomical and/or physiological concerns relevant to speech pathology practice.
Apply knowledge of the physiological processes that support speech, language, and swallowing functions.
Apply knowledge of key anatomical structures involved in speech pathology-related disorders and impairments.
Examine the impact of speech pathology-related disorders and impairments on individuals’ activity and participation across the lifespan.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Anatomy and physiology quiz (2 x 20 minutes)

workload_hours: This unit will have 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week (including 1 hour of lectures, 3 hours of online learning activities, and 2 hours of on-campus workshops). Additionally, there are 6 hours of self-directed study per week, making the total workload 12 hours. Total workload per semester: 144 hours.

title: Linguistics and phonetics
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will gain foundational knowledge in linguistics and phonetics, focusing on the structure and function of language and speech sounds. You will explore key concepts in phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and sociolinguistics and develop skills in transcription using the International Phonetic Alphabet. You will apply linguistic and phonetic principles to analyse speech and language. Through practical exercises and case examples, you will build essential skills required for speech pathology practice in the future.
learning_outcomes: Analyse speech and language samples by applying fundamental knowledge and principles of linguistics;
Acquire transcription skills and apply to speech samples, using the International Phonetic Alphabet;
Discuss how sociolinguistics and cultural, individual and linguistic diversity impact the management of communication difficulties.
Apply fundamental phonetics knowledge and skills when analysing speech production;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Exam (2 hours plus 10 minutes- reading time)
Speech transcription and analysis task (60 minutes)

workload_hours: This unit will have 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week (including 1 hour of lectures, 2 hours of online learning activities, and 3 hours of on-campus workshops). Additionally, there are 6 hours of self-directed study per week, making the total workload of 12 hours per week. Total workload per semester: 144 hours

title: Person centred care and professional practice
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed to build your knowledge about essential principles of assessment and treatment planning in speech pathology practices. You will discuss the impact of communication and swallowing problems on a person’s ability to participate in everyday life. You will learn to apply the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework to interpret communication and swallowing impairments. This approach will help you move beyond isolated symptoms and consider the broader context of an individual’s activities and participation in everyday life. You will develop the ability to formulate intervention goals that are functional and person-centred. You will explore how personal factors, family dynamics, and community resources influence therapy planning and goal achievement. Through your knowledge of these contextual influences, you will be able to apply interventions that are realistic and meaningful for the individuals and their families. You will also be introduced to the principles of different rehabilitation frameworks, which underpin effective intervention strategies. Finally, you will focus on strategies that promote the transfer of communication and swallowing skills from the therapy setting into real-life environments. Through various workshop activities, you will begin translating theoretical knowledge into evidence-informed speech pathology practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss how communication and swallowing impairments can impact an individual’s activity and participation in everyday life.
Discuss how intervention planning and individual goal attainment are influenced by personal, family and community factors.
Apply and discuss different evidence-informed rehabilitation frameworks to enhance functional communication and swallowing outcomes in everyday life.
Formulate evidence-informed interventional goals to support person-centred and responsive care in speech pathology practice.
Apply the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework to interpret communication and swallowing impairments in speech pathology practice.
workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 1 hour of lectures, 3 hours of online learning activities, and 2 hours of workshops. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Speech sound disorders
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will be introduced to the developmental foundations, clinical features, and evidence-based management of speech sound disorders in children. You will explore typical speech sound acquisition and discuss the characteristics and risk factors of speech sound disorders of unknown origin. Furthermore, through case-based learning and practical tasks, you will learn how to compare and contrast evidenced based assessment tools, determine classification subgroups in the diagnosis of speech sound disorders, and evaluate and justify evidence-based intervention approaches. There will also be a focus on how to communicate and collaborate effectively with the client, family and interprofessional team in order to deliver patient centred and culturally responsive care in your management of speech disorders. You will integrate theory with practical application and build your clinical reasoning skills through a variety of teaching and learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and justify evidenced-based intervention approaches for children with speech sound disorders;
Discuss the characteristics and risk factors of speech sound disorders of unknown origin in children;
Compare and contrast evidenced based assessment tools to determine classification subgroups in the differential diagnosis of speech sound disorders;

Communicate and collaborate effectively with the client, their families, and interprofessional teams to facilitate patient-centred and culturally responsive care in the management of speech sound disorders.
Apply knowledge of typical speech sound development in children for the differential diagnosis of speech sound disorders;

assessment_tasks.task_name: VIVA: Intervention planning and roleplay (30 minutes total)
Speech profiling (approximately 1 minute recording and 2,000 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 1 hour of lectures, 3 hours of online learning activities, and 2 hours of workshops. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Introduction to evidence-based practice
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will develop your knowledge and skills in research literacy, which will support clinical decision-making and evidence-based speech pathology practice. You will learn how to combine the different aspects of evidence-based practice in managing communication and swallowing disorders. You will learn how to formulate structured clinical questions, how to identify literature from a range of databases and how to evaluate the quality of selected research papers. Then you will apply findings to support your future learning and practice in the profession of speech pathology.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based decision making to clinical practice and in defined contexts when managing communication and swallowing disorders.
Communicate evidence-based findings related to the management of communication and swallowing disorders to a variety of audiences using different modalities.
Discuss the fundamentals principles of evidence-based practice, inclusive of its role in the profession of speech pathology.
Differentiate between the various levels and types of evidence and its application to research design.
Appraise the quality and relevance of evidence using various appraisal techniques.
workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 1 hour of lectures, 3 hours of online learning activities, and 2 hours of workshops. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Human development and psychology
faculty: School of Primary & Allied Health Care
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will analyse how communication and swallowing develops across the lifespan and illustrate how cultural-linguistic and psychosocial factors shape these processes. You will discuss key psychological theories relevant to speech pathology practice and apply learning theories that facilitate your own professional development and future practice. You will apply this knowledge to contexts relevant to speech pathology practice, strengthening your ability to interpret individual differences in communication and mealtime activities. Throughout the unit, you will also apply effective interpersonal communication and collaboration skills when working within teams.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the relevance of psychological theories within speech pathology practice.
Illustrate how psycho-social and cultural-linguistic factors influence communication and mealtime activities across the lifespan.
Apply reflective practice and learning theories to facilitate your own professional development and future practice.
Apply effective interpersonal communication and collaboration when working in teams.
Analyse the differences in developmental milestones of communication and swallowing across the lifespan.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Exam (2 hours + 10 minutes of reading time)
Human development group presentation (7 minute presentation) and self reflection (200 words)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including 1 hour of lectures, 3 hours of online learning activities, and 2 hours of workshops. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours

title: Designing and conducting health research
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is an introduction to research methods used in health research. It aims to equip you with the theoretical knowledge of research design and methods used in undertaking research, and the practical skills to conduct their own research. You will develop skills in formulating research questions, searching the literature for evidence, identifying and understanding the components of rigorous research design, appropriate data collection and analysis techniques, and ensuring research is conducted in an ethically and culturally sensitive manner. By the end of the unit, you will have the necessary knowledge and skills to initiate their own research project as the basis for a minor thesis, or to conduct a research project within their workplace.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the ethical considerations in promoting ethical conduct in health research;
Critically differentiate between research traditions and methods;
Explain and apply the principles of academic integrity when conducting research.
Formulate a research question that addresses an evidence gap in the health care literature;
Formulate a research protocol that is rigorous and feasible;
Undertake a search and synthesis of the research literature and critically appraise the findings;
Design a research project that includes a method appropriate to the research question;
Communicate the use of research as a basis for decision-making in health care policy & practice;
incompatibilities: SRH5032: Applied research for health practitioners

assessment_tasks.task_name: Research proposal presentation (20 mins and 1000 words)

workload_hours: For this distance education unit, you are expected to undertake your work during private study time. You will be expected to log onto Moodle on a regular basis for announcements and updates. You will need to undertake readings (available via Moodle) and view online materials (e.g. PowerPoint/audio/visual material). You will also be required to undertake regular formative activities. You will be required to undertake all assessment activities as these are all hurdle requirements to ensure that all learning objectives are covered. The assessments will require preparation ranging from readings, writing and undertaking online activities (quizzes and forum discussions).

title: Introduction to research methods for health
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is an introduction to research in health care. You will build your knowledge about the relevant frameworks in constructing an effective research question. You will appraise the literature required to support the research question and distinguish between various methodologies used in research. This unit will support you in differentiating the distinctive elements of a research proposal that will be of assistance to you in your clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply the relevant frameworks to construct an effective research question.
Differentiate the distinctive elements needed for a research proposal.
Compare and contrast various databases to appraise the literature required to support an effective research question.
Examine ethical issues that may arise in different types of research.
Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative methodologies required for research.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Literature review (1500 words) and video presentation (no more than 5 minutes)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher directed study per week including Moodle content, readings, online media and assessment tasks, 1 hour of online tutorials led by teacher each week, 1 hour of online workshop/applied activities led by teacher each week 6 hours per week of self-directed study Total per week = 12 hours

title: Applied research for health
school: Faculty of Medicine, Nursing and Health Sciences
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed to support in the preparation for the independent research project. The unit will facilitate the capacity to translate thoughts and interests around health care into a sound research project by undertaking a critical review of the literature, and developing a research proposal which is feasible and ethical.
learning_outcomes: Explain how the use of research is a basis for decision making in the health care policy and clinical arena particularly in its application to health care practice;
Critically analyse the research literature in response to the proposed research question;
Formulate a research question that addresses an evidence gap in health care;
Develop a feasible and ethical research proposal for implementation within a health or community setting to address a novel research question.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Research question and rationale (1,000 words equiv.- including demonstrated use of PICOT or equiv.)
Research proposal (3,000 words equiv. including GANTT chart & budget table)

workload_hours: 6 hours of teacher-directed study per week, including a weekly online tutorial and an online individual application discussion via an open calendar booking system. Teacher-directed learning and activities occur via Moodle. 6 hours per week of self-directed study. Total per week = 12 hours
